# The packages under `internal/`

**Every package states its own rationale in its package doc.** `go doc ./internal/coord` is the authority on coordination, not this file. What follows is a map, so you know which doc to read, and each row carries what its package decided that a reader would be tempted to "fix" back to the obvious shape, together with what the obvious alternative cost when it was tried. None of it binds: change the code, and rewrite the comment and the row, in the same commit. A new package gets a row.

## The spine — what everything else is built on

| Package | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `queue` | THE EventQueue contract. One interface, two backends (`memory`, `jetstream`), both certified by ONE suite in `queuetest`. A SEAT'S INBOX IS TWO MAILBOXES UNDER ONE SUBSCRIPTION (`lane.go`): a wake marked `Prioritize` rides the inbox's priority lane, every drain takes the lane first, and every verb that manages or holds the subscription acts on both, so a held seat holds a person's message with the rest of its mail. THE DRAIN WINDOW BOUNDS WHAT ONE TURN IS HANDED: an inbox event of a priority partition inside the drain's cap joins it, and one deeper is delivered in its own turn, exactly once, never reached for, because settling mail the consumer never delivered sits outside its acknowledgement state. A REQUEUE KEEPS A PARTITION WHOLE (`Together`): a partition holding a priority event goes back to the lane as one unit. `Waiting` counts what a subscription holds that no handler OF THE ASKING CLIENT is running on, per mailbox, which is why only the node holding a seat can report its inbox honestly (the engine's `seat_inbox_waiting` reports). Nineteen verbs, and FOUR of them are the opposite of every other: `Ask` (and `AskEach`, which hands each reply over as it arrives) and `Serve` are an EPHEMERAL scatter (core NATS request/reply on the real backend: no stream, no consumer, no ack, no retention, no publish listener) because a query is not an event, and a search fan-out on the durable verbs would write two records and an audit row per keystroke; `Broadcast` and `Listen` are the same shape as a fan-out (core publish and subscribe, at most once, every listener hears every message, one at a time per listener, refused with `ErrUnavailable` rather than buffered into a reconnect), which presence travels on because a heartbeat on a durable verb would be a replicated write per cursor move. An answerer answers CONCURRENTLY, up to the bound its REGISTRATION states through ONE `AnswerGate` implementation both backends share — a gate per registration, so a request waiting for a slot waits behind its own registration's answers and never another's, in a buffer its backend bounds (the NATS client's 64 MiB and 500 000 messages a subscription, past which a request is dropped as a slow consumer and its asker hears nothing, so a registration whose requests are large and whose answers wait answers past what it holds AT ONCE, as estate's engine writes' lane does); `ConcurrentAnswers` (64) for an answerer whose answers are work done now, and for one whose answers WAIT in a queue of their own the bound of that queue, on a registration of its own, since a slot held through a wait is one every other request of its registration waits behind; a bound below one is refused (`ErrAnswerBound`) — and a withdrawal waits for what is in flight: run inside the subscription callback, every request to an answerer waited behind the one before it while the twin answered in parallel and certified it clean. Nothing above this package may branch on which backend is running. A durable subscription IS a seat's mailbox: it exists without a consumer and retains what is published while nothing is attached — and it outlives every record of its own name, a removed seat's handle included, so the BROKER has to be able to list them (`ListSubscriptions`) or a leaked mailbox can never be found again. Handlers have three outcomes — ack, nak, and *defer*. A failed verb is MARKED with one of three sentinels and nothing else may be branched on — `ErrTooLarge` (permanent), `ErrNotLive` (consumes nothing until started again; a connection NATS closed for good is one, `jetstream.ErrConnectionLost`) and `ErrUnavailable` (the broker did not answer — a CONDITION, never proof of teardown; `Ask` refuses rather than buffer its request into a down connection, and a `DeleteSubscription` the broker cannot hear has still detached); the suite holds both backends to it through the `BrokerDown` capability. Attachment has four verbs of differing destructiveness, because `unsubscribe` never said which one it was — and only `Stop`, never `Detach`, also ends an idle consume loop's outstanding fetch, since the connection closes next anyway: a loop parked in a fetch noticed its cancellation only when the fetch ran out, so every stop of a queue with an idle attachment waited out a poll it then abandoned. Its real backend's test support is THREE packages and deliberately not one: `jetstream/jetstreamtest` stands up a multi-member cluster, and importing it IS declaring one (see `solo`), so the single EXTERNAL server a suite restarts under a running client with another `max_payload` is `jetstream/externaltest`, which requires `externaltest.Token` unless a case starts it `Anonymous`., and the ONE SIZE a test broker declares is `jetstream/brokertest` (`StoreMaxBytes`), because every embedded fixture — a node's, a cluster member's, a lone domain log's — needs that figure, and importing the first declares a solo suite while the second is the external server alone. A TEST'S BROKER IS NEVER SIZED FROM THE DISK: an unset limit is three quarters of the free space on a volume every package beside it shares, and a fresh node reserves several gibibytes before it does anything, so a boot passed or failed on how full the runner was; a declared limit is accounting, which nats-server never checks against the disk. So a TEST BINARY REFUSES TO START an embedded broker with a store directory and no limit (`jetstream.ErrUndeclaredSize`, checked in `startEmbedded`, where every way of starting one arrives, so no list of fixtures can go stale), and the one case that may leave it to nats-server is one whose subject is that derivation, started under `jetstream.SizedByTheDisk`; a server a case builds from nats-server's own options never reaches that start, so `brokertest`'s `TestEveryNATSServerATestBuildsDeclaresItsSize` reads every Go file of the module and fails an Options literal, a function assigning an Options value's store or a nats-server configuration that enables JetStream or gives it a store directory and states no limit — the value judged by its type (`sourcetree/decltype`, in a world that reads each package as its tests compile it, so an Options a test helper of another file returns is typed too) rather than by a list, and a configuration by nats-server's own parser. The exemptions it replaced — a broker that reserves nothing, a case that reserves only what is left — were free to drop, since declaring costs nothing, and the fixtures that had gone undeclared were not the exempt ones. `StoreIn` sets a node's store directory and the size TOGETHER, because the directory is what turns the limit into a derivation from its volume; `GitletCacheIn` declares the cache budget and transfer lane of a node serving Gitlet beside them, because a cache left to derive its budget gets the room the declared limit leaves on the runner's disk, which a smaller runner does not have; `jetstreamtest`'s members take the figure unless their base states one; the shared fixtures of `engine` and `cmd/crewlet` and the cluster harness each have a case that goes red when they lose it, and `engine`'s `TestTheTestBrokerSizeHoldsAFreshNode` is the failure that names the cause and the constant when the register outgrows the figure, which then refuses every boot on every machine rather than only on a small disk. `externaltest`'s server has a fixed cap and its account states `StoreMaxBytes`, which a node reads back as an operator's limit; `StartUnstated` is the broker that states none. An embedded member LOCKS its configured store directory (`StoreDirLock`, through `flock`) before the server exists and lets it go only once it has stopped: nats-server accepts a second broker on one directory and both write it, and the node database's lock cannot stand in, because the engine starts its broker before it opens that database and the two paths are independent settings. EVERY CONNECTION THE ENGINE OPENS TO ITS OWN EMBEDDED BROKER IS IN PROCESS, a clustered member's too: its client listener is open only because nats-server routes once one is, so it binds `127.0.0.1` and advertises nothing (`Cluster.NoAdvertise`) — dialled over TCP, it bound every interface and gossiped every member's client URL to any client. AND EVERY CONNECTION PRESENTS A KEY (ADR-0094, `brokerauth.go`, `fleetauth.go`): every embedded broker installs ONE authenticator through nats-server's embedding hooks, which admits a route presenting the username and password derived from a key of `secrets.keys`, a leaf link or an operator on a member's loopback client listener presenting the nkey derived from one and signing its nonce, and this process's own in-process clients signing with a key minted at each start (the engine's on the global account, the membership code's on `$SYS`) — every key of the ring accepted, the active one presented, so the keyring's rotation moves the broker with no step of its own; nats-server's own blocks are not used because none carries a rotation without a secret on the wire or an anonymous path. Refusals are `broker_peer_refused` (once a minute a class, naming the key) and `crewlet.broker.peer.refusals`; the broker's own per-attempt authentication line is DEBUG, and it encrypts nothing, so ADR-0031's signing stands. An EXTERNAL server is admitted only where the INFO it sends says it authenticates its clients — `auth_required`, or `tls_required` with `tls_verify`, never a certificate this node presents to a server that does not verify it — read off the plaintext handshake by the dial's recording dialer, since nats.go parses no `tls_verify` (`requiresAuthentication`, `ErrUnauthenticatedBroker`), after the max_payload contract and on every connection `dial` opens — the INFO of the server the client is on when the dial completes, matched by its server_id rather than taken from the newest connection a reconnect may have opened, and a client on no server by then refused as a lost connection; an INFO it did not read is a refusal. That dialer also resolves a member's name itself (`nats.SkipHostLookup`), shuffles its addresses and shares one 2 s connect budget among them, as the client's own dialer did, which a custom dialer replaces. `OpenCoordination` reaches the broker for its coordination store ALONE — dials an external one, or starts and owns an embedded one with the same readiness waits a queue makes — and builds no queue, because a queue PROVISIONS the engine's streams. A state log's `DomainLog`, the backend's seam outside the contract, reports how many members store its stream (`DomainLog.Members`, the factor the broker last reported, which the read index judges an unconfirmed barrier by), and also WATCHES (`DomainLog.Watch`): for a reader that keeps its work in rows and only wants to hear sooner which object moved (Gitlet's home node), one ephemeral consumer takes each new record's SUBJECT and sequence and never its body — headers only, from the log's end, acknowledging nothing, one replica in memory, reaped a minute after nobody pulls (`ephemeralInactive`, the live feed's minute) — because carrying a domain's records (the code log's up to 8 MiB) to every watcher would cost each the log's whole volume again. What it may have missed it says (`Gap`), with how far on the log that reaches, and never repairs: a lost consumer — two missed heartbeats, a pull nobody serves, the broker's word — is replaced by one of its own at the log's end, whose create's own reply names the position it begins after; a delivery the consumer counted and this node never received keeps the consumer and reaches the revealing delivery's position; a reconnect keeps it too and reaches the log's end, read once the reconnect is noticed. The caller waits for its copy to reach that position, then reads its rows — the records a gap held may be ones its copy has not applied yet, and rows read before them find nothing to do — so a nudge only ever shortens a wait. A HAND-BACK SAYS WHY: `Defer` takes a `DeferCause` from a closed set beside its free-text reason, which is what a report of a message its hand-backs retired may name. DEAD LETTERS ARE ONE PLACE (`KeepDeadLetter`; `DeadLettersOn`, listing each `Kept` entry's sequence, stored instant, expiry and bytes; `DropDeadLetter`): a subscription's budget and a reader that settles its own deliveries — a wake feed, whose consumer is a state log's rather than a subscription — keep them alike, on JetStream in `CREWLET_DLQ`, kept by the event stream's age and listed one entry at a time from the stream's LEADER (a replica behind would show a kept entry as gone to the reader that counts what vanished as expired), on the twin in the broker under the same retention; the twin KEEPS a publish to a dead-letter subject too, as the broker's age-kept stream does, where it once dropped it unsubscribed. |
| `coord` | Cross-process ownership: TTL leases with a monotonic fencing epoch, plus everything else a fleet has to agree on (`fleet.go`). THE DOCUMENT FAMILIES ARE GONE, both native backends left them for ordered logs, and what survived is the KEY GRAMMAR (`keys.go`), because every class the fleet still writes composes an id, a stream name or a node id into a subject token path and each of those can carry a byte a token cannot, the activation pointer (a COMPARE-AND-SET: there is no leader, so the flip is what stops two operators overwriting each other, and the sealed company document rides INSIDE its record as a JSON object, because as a key of its own a racing writer's body replaced the one the winning flip named; and its expectation is STRICT on both backends, ADR-0057: a write expecting a revision lands only while the pointer names it, and a pointer deleted or purged since the read is a race rather than nothing to have raced with, because every caller reads the pointer first and passes `ExpectAbsent` when it read none, and under the lenient rule this replaced the KV backend refused that write over the removal marker while the twin landed it, a 409 on every config write for up to three hours and a quarter; only `crewlet run -import-company` passes neither) and per-node apply status (which names the revision the node SERVES beside the one its epoch asked for, because the two differ exactly on a node that refused the fleet's revision, the epoch it last APPLIED beside the one it attempted, because a refusal says the node did not reach that epoch and never which one it did reach, and the one it BOOTS ON beside both, because the boot row moves only after an apply has succeeded and that write is local and best effort, so a node runs a revision it would not restart on for as long as a failed write takes to repair — and a reader keeping what a node needs in order to start, which the Kubernetes operator does with a revision's sealed credentials, would otherwise drop exactly what its next boot needs; `GET /fleet` reports all three per node), the completion ledger, the delivery dedupe, the custody claims (which one data node keeps each batch of a stateless node's events), the fixed-window COUNTER (`Counter.Allow`, each key carrying its window's width) in two buckets: windows up to `MaxRateWindow`, one minute, in `crewlet_rate`, the notification valve's and the Dashboard Assistant's per-person turn rate, a bucket that keeps a few multiples of that widest window, bounded by the age it actually holds; and windows up to `MaxCounterWindow`, a UTC day, in `crewlet_counter_windows`, aged three days, the remote check cells' box-minutes, since either age in the other's bucket is wrong: a day's count reaped between its charges, or a minute's record kept for days; both backends refuse a wider window rather than restart its count mid-window, the TOKEN COUNTERS (one record per scope, `org`, a seat's `agent:` or, where a company caps the assistant, a person's `person:`, with a slot per calendar window, day, ISO week, month on the company's clock, each carrying its window's LABEL, so the roll onto a new window happens inside the compare-and-swap that counts the charge and there is no reset of any kind, ADR-0019 — and written by ONE compare-and-swap per node per scope however many charges the node has in flight: coalesced and decided in arrival order, each exactly as a serial order would, because every round of every seat writes the company's record and a write per round made every round in flight a contender no attempt bound covers; every compare-and-swap loop on a fleet record is bounded by its HEAD COUNT, the nodes writing the key, with a wait counted in the round trips the node measures on the bucket, never by a constant below its writers), the capacity window (ONE record that is both the operation and the exclusion, beside the per-node admissions and acknowledgements the handshake is made of), the OBJECT STORE's backend record (create-only, compared at every boot, so a node naming another store refuses to start rather than splitting the files between two) and its collector's last report (and NO LOCK of any kind on an object, since a key named only by the write that uploaded it leaves a deletion nothing to race, ADR-0027), which seats a person PAUSED (one compare-and-set record per seat, filed under the seat's ID, as the inbox it holds is named; with no age, because an expiring pause is a resume nobody chose; every node watches them, holds a paused seat's inbox and takes that hold again before attaching a paused seat it acquires), each human seat's CHAT READ STATE (its person's read cursors, per-room mutes and do-not-disturb, one record per seat merged forward under a compare-and-set so two tabs never lose each other's progress — kept under `iam.RecordOwner`, so the seat's next holder inherits it as it does the seat's inbox; every node serving sockets WATCHES them and pushes a changed record to that seat's own tabs, derived from the record rather than told by the node that took the write, through the one watch the pauses use (`kv/watch.go`); with no age, because an expired cursor marks a room its reader had finished as unread; and in a bucket of its OWN although its retention is the positions register's, because it is the busiest record the fleet writes and as a class there its flushes would share the one raft group and leader the trim's inputs go through) and the company's SECRETS, last-write-wins for an operator's rotation, with a version on every row and the conditional writes (`CreateSecret`, `UpdateSecret`) the engine's own key material and a rekey need, a create for a company key's mint, an update at the version a rekey read, since a plain put of a key is how two minters each derive under their own, and a plain write of what a rekey read undoes whatever landed in between. A RESOURCE NAME IS SEGMENTED for the same reason, `seat:<id>` is the two segments `seat` and the seat's id (derived from its immutable handle, ADR-0013, so a lease, a mailbox and a pause all name a seat the same way on every node), so its lease and epoch keys carry the CLASS as a subject token and `ListLive`/`PreferredResources` take a `Class` rather than a prefix string: the membership read asks the broker for one class, the presence leases, instead of every lease in the fleet, and the sweep's hints for the seats instead of every epoch the deployment has ever minted. There is deliberately NO all-classes listing and no empty segment, because both fail the same silent way, a filter matching nothing answers exactly like a class with no members, and `seat:` writes a key nothing can decode, so the lease lands and no listing ever returns it, which every node reads as a free seat. One class is the PROCESS'S rather than a seat's, a node's or a duty's: `taker:<incarnation>` (`ClassTaker`), the sandbox's word that a process still keeps the executor sessions it began taking, claimed afresh by every process, so it counts its tokens on ONE counter for the whole class (`CounterResource`, which both backends mint through) — a counter per taker would leave a record per process start in the ageless epochs bucket — and its own key is in the duty bucket, whose age removes it three hours after its last write. A lease whose work goes on only inside the window its renewals confirm is renewed `KeptRenewals` times a TTL — the engine's kept duties and the taker lease, one count for both. Every "do I hold this?" is three-valued, held / definitively not / **unknown**, and treating unknown as loss tears a healthy company down over a two-second store blip. A LISTING IS THREE-VALUED TOO, every key live throughout it, or unknown, never a shorter list, and on the KV backend that is CERTIFIED rather than trusted, because a pass cannot tell it is complete: a renew rewrites a key behind the marker that ends the pass, and 848 of 3,634 membership reads missed a live lease. So each listing reads the stream's key index beside the pass and reads again, from the stream LEADER, every key the index names that the pass lost or delivered only as a delete marker, never through the bucket's own get, a direct get that a replica behind the quorum answers "not found", and a marker because a replica behind a re-creation serves one for a key live throughout, and an index answered while the stream has no leader is refused, so an election is unknown rather than a short fleet. A pass that goes five seconds without a delivery once the index has answered (`passIdle`, the client's own idle-heartbeat interval) is ENDED and certified, because the client's end marker never comes for a pass whose pending messages were removed before it reached them. The removal MARKERS that re-read pays for are swept by the maintenance duty from every ageless bucket after `MarkerRetention` (three hours, which is `MaxDutyTTL`), each purged through its own revision: a COST bound, never a correctness one, since no read here takes a marker as an answer and a create asks the leader what the key holds rather than conditioning on a marker a sweep may already have removed. Retention here is a BUCKET's age, never a per-write TTL, a delivery CLAIM included: it carries its own deadline only so that a lapsed claim is taken over by a compare-and-set, while the claims bucket's age (`MaxClaimTTL`, set by the longest claim anybody takes) is what removes it, and a claim asking for longer is refused rather than clamped. The DETACHED EXECUTORS' record (`SandboxRuns`) is the one opaque value here, what a job can make large kept BESIDE it as PARTS, each under a key of its own (`SandboxRunPart`, `MutateSandboxRunPart`, one of `coord.RunParts()`: `RunLog`, the bridged tool log, and `RunHanded`, the sealed secrets a job's box was handed; on the KV a second subject token, so a listing of records filtered on `*` never reads one) — each written only beside a record (a create that finds the record gone after it removes itself), EVERY part removed with the record by its delete unless a record of the turn's next run stands beside it again by then (each part is read, then the record, and purged only through the revision read), and, where a node stopped between the removals, any part left without a record removed by the marker sweep, off the same pass of the runs' bucket its markers are found in — an update of a part so left is still taken until then, which nothing reads, since every reader comes through a record — and every change after its create is a DECISION its caller hands to `MutateSandboxRun`, which the store takes again on the record as it then stands whenever another writer landed first — through `casRetry`, within the bound every fleet key shares (`fleetCASAttempts`, twice `fleetWriters`, each attempt after a loss waiting a window of round trips), which outlasts the overlap of the calls one run's box can make at once, since one run's record takes every tool call its box makes over the bridge, from as many as twenty subagents at once, and a bound exhausted is `coord.ErrUnavailable`, never a refusal; the memory twin decides outside its lock too, so a decision asked twice is what every test sees as well. A run is WATCHED by its own key (`WatchSandboxRun`): its first state certified as a listing's answer is, then each later state, a closed channel meaning "stopped hearing", never a delete. `NodeStatus` also carries each node's own `api.auth.admin` POSTURE (`serve` or `refuse`, meta key `admin`), absent rather than empty on a node that serves no API, because the posture is applied at decision time and never written, so a fleet mid-rollout legally disagrees and nothing else would say so; `/query/fleet` reports it per node. It carries the ALARMS firing on the node too (`alarms`: one `AlarmMark` per kind, its kind and since when, the longest-standing first, off the node's own tracker), so every node's set is read at once and as it stands rather than only by whoever is looking at that node; behind a flag of its own (`AlarmsEvaluated`) rather than a nil list, because "nothing is firing" and "no table evaluated" are opposite claims and a nil slice is also what collecting nothing produces; and the kind and the start only, never the measurement, which moves on every evaluation. And BESIDE the status, never in it, a Gitlet node's presence row carries what its git cache gives its BACKGROUND WORK (`GitBackgroundKey`, `git_background_bytes`: the cache's maintenance budget, re-read every maintenance pass), which every Gitlet node weighs every other by to place a repository's maintenance (`estate.Router.Maintainer`) rather than asking each in turn — outside the status because a beat whose status hook overran drops the status whole, and a placement input dropped with it would leave the node saying nothing of what it can hold for that beat; the seat host writes it on EVERY beat from memory, ZERO INCLUDED (a Gitlet node with nothing to give says so), so a row without it is a node NOT SAYING (`GitBackgroundFromMeta`'s false), never one with nothing to give; read through the one `intFromMeta`, since every target is 64-bit. A roster asked PER REQUEST is a LEASE VIEW (`view.go`): listed once a heartbeat and answered from memory, and WATCHED between listings (`WatchLive`, every claim, renewal and release of one class as the holder it left, narrowed at the broker like a listing) — a write that disagrees with the last listing lists again at once, held to `MinViewRefresh`, and a renewal that agrees lists nothing — because a view that only listed learned of a join a heartbeat late, and a fleet booted at once, every first listing taken before any presence lease existed, routed for its first heartbeat as though each node were alone: a data node committed every push it received itself, and a node without `data` refused every push, fetch and read. The watch is begun before the first listing and is a HINT, never the answer, since a lapse is no write: the cadence still drops a node that stopped without releasing. A positions row read back carries the instant the STORE took it (`NodePositions.StoredAt` — on the KV backend the entry's own timestamp, the broker's clock — filled by every listing and never written) beside the writer's own stamp, so every row read back says how far its writer's clock stands from the broker's with no request of its own, and a register's rows, one broker clock storing them all, say how far each node's clock stands from the others': what the engine's `clock_skew` alarm compares against their median. A node's MODELS ride its presence lease beside its MCP servers (`NodeStatus.Models`, `NodeStatus.Runners`): one row per entry with only a 12-character prefix of its sign-in id, bounded text, never a fan-out. Two model classes live in the positions register, one record per entry: `llm_retry` (a person's retry, the later stamp kept, applied by its stamp) and `llm_device_sign_in` (a device sign-in in progress, whose lifetime is a record field its readers keep, since a bucket age restarts at every update). Two MCP classes live there too (ADR-0074): `mcp_listing`, one node's listing of one server, written under the node's PRESENCE EPOCH and counted only while that presence holds at that epoch (`LiveMCPListings`, the one filter), and `mcp_schema`, a tool definition's schemas stored once, create-only, under its digest; both bounded by the store as well as the writer, a listing's server and node stamped from its key, and the schemas one listing stores held to `MaxMCPListingSchemaBytes` (1 MiB) in all by the node that builds it. `mcp_restart` (`mcprestart.go`) is a person's request to restart an MCP server, one record per server and per seat named, a STAMP like a model retry (every node restarts what began before it, the later stamp wins, no age). `MCPInstance` (`mcpinstance.go`) is the wire shape of one instance's health between nodes, answered at query time and never stored, and the heartbeat's MCP row carries only its bounded summary (`down_since`, `error_class`, `restarts`). `mcp_check` (`mcpcheck.go`) is each MCP server's LATEST TEST, the current value only (the later test wins, no age), bounded by its writer to 32 nodes and 512-byte sentences and refused by `Validate` past that; never its tools. `mcp_accepted` (`mcpaccepted.go`) is the DEFINITION EACH MCP TOOL'S LEVEL WAS DECIDED ON, one record per (server, the server's own name for the tool), written by COMPARE-AND-SET at the version read (zero creates only), its words bounded as a listing's; a removal accepted keeps its record, marked, so a server stays baselined (ADR-0078). `mcp_oauth` and `mcp_sign_in` (`mcpoauth.go`) are each MCP server's OAuth grant, its PUBLIC half only (who signed in, the issuer and client, the scopes, when it runs out, the vendor's words for a renewal refused for good, never a token), watched by every node, and a sign-in in progress, whose PKCE verifier and client are sealed in it and whose state is spent by moving it on at the version read; the sealed half of a grant is `fleetsecrets.Estate`'s (ADR-0075). |
| `store` | The node's LOCAL databases: its OWN file (the audit event log, learning memory, config revisions), brought up by `OpenNode`, and the REPLICATED estate beside it — everything a state log's applier writes — opened on that handle by the engine (`OpenReplicated`; an adoption closes it with `CloseReplicated` and opens it again). Every data node holds it from boot whatever its company runs — holding is the node's, and `engine.HoldsEstate` is the one answer the engine and the backup read (`crewlet migrate` reaches it through Tier A's rule that a node without `data` is scratch, and refuses a scratch store), so a backup copies what the node holds and refuses a held estate that is closed at that instant. Two files because a snapshot is a copy of ONE of them: taken from a single file it would be a copy of everything followed by a delete, and with no in-place `VACUUM` the audit log's pages ride along in the artifact, the transfer, the checksum and the integrity check. A COPY (`Backup`, which a donor's snapshot and a fleet backup both take) is ONE MOMENT holding every commit that returned before it began, and that is `vacuumInto`'s doing rather than the driver's: the driver's `VACUUM INTO` takes no view of its own — its deferred `BEGIN` takes no snapshot and its reads are nested statements that begin none — so it copied whatever view the drawn connection's previous read had left (measured under a committing writer: 143 of 300 copies missed a commit that had returned before them, while 0 of 300 657 reads on the same pool did) with nothing holding that view against a checkpoint (6 of 150 copies torn, two tables one transaction wrote held at two values). A copy now holds a read transaction on a connection of its own — outside the pool, so one copy never needs two readers at once, which `TestACopyTakesOneConnectionFromItsPool` holds by standing a copy of a node file opened at `store.max_open_conns: 1` and two at once of the replicated estate at its two-reader floor at their `VACUUM INTO` together (`storetest.CopyHold`) — then takes the copying connection's view, then copies, at the cost of no checkpoint past that moment while it runs — the live `-wal` grows by what the node commits meanwhile, so a copy is LISTED while it holds the log (`DB.Copies`) and MEASURES how far the log grew under it before its hold ends, as a share of the file it copied (`DB.CopyHoldsBack`: what a copy taken now is expected to hold back on the file's own volume, the last copy that finished being the measure and none until one has; copies.go), and `VolumeFree` is what a volume has free — what an unprivileged process may still write there — as both judgements of that room read it, the donor snapshot's gate and the fleet backup's; `TestTheDriversVacuumIntoStillCopiesItsConnectionsLastView` is the tripwire for the day the driver does this itself. No transaction spans the two, no read joins across them and nothing `ATTACH`es — a static walk holds it. The replicated estate reaches a caller as one of two TYPES: `ReplicatedHandle`, which can write and which only the framework, the appliers, the runtime and two named exceptions hold, and `ReplicatedReader`, which every reader is handed and whose one transaction the engine runs with writes refused (`query_only`) — so who can write it is a property of the type before `TestOnlyTheApplierWritesTheReplicatedEstate` reads the code, and `TestOnlyTheRuntimeReachesTheReplicatedEstate` keeps the reach through the node's own store to the runtime, the backup and the operator's offline commands, since a node without `data` has no file to reach. Each file's pool is its ORDINARY READERS — `store.max_open_conns`, or `max(8, GOMAXPROCS)` unset (two dashboards' worth of socket queries; the floor, `MinReaderConns`, is also the most pages the smallest data node scans at once, which a Gitlet node's full reads are held to: `code/cache.MaxFullRounds`), never under two on the replicated estate — PLUS one connection held from open for identity work (`store.Identity`), so no read burst can starve the lookup that answers who is acting, PLUS one pinned writer per log the replicated estate carries: every one ADDED on top rather than taken out of the readers, an explicit setting included, because one taken out is a read burst queueing behind it with nothing naming the loss. Every connection of either file keeps the same 32 MiB page cache. **One file, one process** — exclusively owned, so nothing here has to be safe against a peer, and the migrator's advisory-lock idiom simply disappears: a migration run is serialised by the FILE's own claim, one run per path at a time, never by one lock for the process, behind which a test package spent most of its wall clock queued. The runner applies what THIS binary carries and STEPS OVER a version it does not — a newer build's, before a rollback — so the node boots, and `ForeignMigrations` (on the replicated estate's read-only `ReplicatedReader` too) names what it stepped over for the one caller that must not act as if those tables were empty: the object store's collector. The driver's capabilities are MEASURED ONCE PER PROCESS (`caps.go`) and reported on every open — the binary decides them, not the file — and `MaxVariables` reads the probe's own 32 766 ceiling, which the pinned driver reaches, so what bounds an applier's statement is `RowsPerInsert`'s 1 000-row cap (it used to read 2 000, the driver's limit on result COLUMNS, and every applier chunked to that). `InsertRows` is the one way an applier writes a collection, a statement a chunk; `InsertRowsReturning` is the same chunks QUERIED, for a writer that must know WHICH rows it wrote — under `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` a chunk's count says how many it skipped and never which (`internal/code`'s notices, which name only rows their transaction wrote). Anything the COMPANY has to agree on belongs in `coord` instead, and migrations 0010–0013 are what that rule cost when it was broken. The config history is that rule's sharpest case (`Configs`, ADR-0057): WHICH revision is the company is `coord`'s activation pointer, and `company_config` holds only this node's own facts about it, kept apart since node migration 0052 — the revision it BOOTS on (`is_active`, moved online by `Serve` alone), the FLEET's revision as it last saw it, runnable here or not (`is_fleets`, `SawFleet`), and an OFFLINE OFFER not yet published with the base it was built on and the instant the boot planned for it (`offered`, `offered_over`, `offered_at`). One column used to say all three, so a node that refused a revision booted on it at its next start and was refused before the engine ran, a write was walked back by a tick a moment behind, and an offline change was published over a fleet that had moved on. `Restorable` is the company as the node knows it when the pointer is gone (an offer built on the fleet's row, or on anything where the node has seen no fleet's row, else the fleet's row, else the boot row: a node that refused R and runs P restores R), and `Purge` keeps the boot row, the fleet's row, the chain behind each, read inside the deleting transaction, and every revision activated inside the window, whatever its creation date. One driver: `OpenNode`, `OpenReplicated` and `Pending` reach a connection through ONE helper, because the second path was the one that skipped the native-library preparation and panicked. A node without the `data` role opens `Scratch` (the file DISCARDED under the store's own lock before it is opened, so a database another process or another handle holds is refused rather than deleted beneath it; the handle says so, `DB.Scratch`, the one reading of the fact that cannot disagree with what the open did, which is where the reconciler learns that the boot row it writes outlives nothing) and holds no replicated estate, so a path that reaches for it is told `ErrNoEstate` rather than handed an empty database that reads as a company with nothing in it. And a replicated estate that is NOT OPEN answers `ErrNoEstate` rather than crashing — not open is a legitimate, documented state (a node without `data`, an adoption between its rename and its reopen, and after `Close`), so a goroutine already in flight reaches it honestly; the open handle sits in an atomic slot for the same reason, since an adoption swaps it while readers are running. A write whose line never reached the lock gives up with `ErrBusy`, the one failure here a caller clears by trying again. `Probe` asks a node database's lock WITHOUT OPENING THE FILE AND WITHOUT KEEPING THE CLAIM — how a `crewlet` command learns whether the engine runs — because opening the file to learn it would migrate a database the command never reads (and create one on a node that never booted), and keeping the claim would make a second command read the first as a running engine. A `code_fetched` event's fields are PROMOTED to `read_*` columns as it is written (node/0061, and node/0062 its `reads`, node/0015's idiom), so a day's reads of unit repositories (`UsageDay.RepoReads`) group on columns rather than extracting JSON from every payload and SUM each record's reads — a record is a reader's reads of a flush, and one counting none is left out: a busy day of 50 000 such records adds 116 ms to its derivation (`BenchmarkUsageForDay`), whatever each counts, against 272 ms read out of the payload, under the 150 ms the publisher's tick allows. A seat's changes opened, reviews given and findings received (`UsageSeat.Code`) are read OUT OF THE PAYLOADS of `change_opened` and `review_submitted` instead — each the agent ids it counts on, findings on the change's owner — each change and review counted once by its id: a seat opens and reviews at most a change a turn, so a day holds a few of them against the tens of thousands of rows the read columns were promoted for. `Hold` is its opposite, for the one caller that must exclude another process while holding no handle: `crewlet run` keeps the claim from the read it decides what to boot on with until the engine has opened the same file, so no offline command can write the row the boot already decided on, and the engine's own open shares the claim it gives back. |
| `statelog` | The durable-state framework, with TWELVE domains on it — the tracker, the knowledge base, the identity estate, the artifacts, their datastore, the Dashboard Assistant's conversations, chat, the seats' executor sessions, Gitlet and the seats' access history strictly ordered and claiming identity, the vectors and each data node's usage compacted and claiming neither — and each domain is a site in several per-domain lists across the tree that fail SILENTLY when a thirteenth is added and one is missed. One ordered stream per domain is the write-ahead log, N identical SQL copies are the durable state, and the checkpoint commits in the same transaction as the rows. A READER WAITS ON THE REACHED POSITION, NEVER THE CHECKPOINT (`Runner.Reached`: every record at or below it committed, or a barrier the loop decoded and verified, which writes no row on any node): the loop releases a read the moment it decodes the barriers before it, and commits a run of nothing but barriers in the ONE checkpoint transaction it keeps beside it, never inline, coalescing whatever arrives while it runs — committed inline, a checkpoint that wrote no row put a disk's stalled fsync in front of every linearizable read (its own barrier's commit, the barrier's before it, and every barrier that arrived meanwhile, undecoded) and answered them `behind` at `ReadBudget` with every row already on the node. A barrier that does not commit is judged by how many members store its log (`NewReadIndex` takes the count, the engine handing it `jetstream.DomainLog.Members` — the stream's own replication factor, kept by every state read, never Tier A's floor on it): `no_quorum` on several, and on ONE never that, with no majority to miss and no election to wait — `broker_stalled` where its time ran out (the member's own write held, a disk behind the fsync `stream.sync: always` makes; final for every node, hinted one `DefaultBarrierBudget`) and `broker_unreachable` where it ended on an error. Everything durable still reads the committed checkpoint — the heartbeat's `Stance`, the trim floor, a restart, the write fence — and acknowledgements follow the commit, so a restart is handed the reached-but-uncommitted barriers again. A DOMAIN THAT STAMPS ITS OWN ANSWER — Gitlet's snapshot a cache asks its next delta from — reads through `Reader.ReadThrough`, handed the checkpoint row its transaction reads CARRIED to the reached position the read was released at: the later of the two names the rows exactly, everything between them a barrier, while the row alone lags every barrier its node has decoded and not committed, and two nodes stamped one object's rows in the wrong order. A DOUBT GIVES IT ALL BACK: at a moment after which the log may be another history — a failed fetch, an end read below what the loop holds — the reached position goes back to the checkpoint and every record held past it (in the loop's hands, the reorder buffer, waiting beside it, and a failed pull's own buffer) goes back to the broker unapplied (`Message.Release`), after the checkpoint transaction in flight returns, before the checkpoint's record is verified — one record vouches for the log only up to itself, so kept, the old history's records were applied past it and the restored log's at their sequences dropped as redeliveries. Where the rows last CHANGED is a third position (`Runner.Changed`), which no barrier moves, for a cache keyed on the rows — the knowledge answers' — which, keyed on either of the other two, every linearizable read in the fleet retired. NOT the store's own WAL — that is Turso's local journal, per file and invisible to any peer; this is an APPLICATION log a fleet derives its SQL state from, and the two share only a word. The write authority is one sentence — take ONE snapshot of your own rows, decide and form the expectation inside it, publish, let the broker arbitrate, never guess — and every clause buys a specific failure: a second read pairs an old decision with a new expectation and the broker accepts it, and an expectation formed from `version` rather than from the ARBITRATION ANCHOR wedges on the one case a gate creates. A write that cannot carry one expectation is SEQUENCED instead (`PatternSequenced`: the artifact datastore and chat's messages): it publishes with no expectation, the log orders it, its applier decides it from the record and its own rows and owes a VERDICT ROW for every record, and its writer reads that row back by operation id before it answers — because the applier's own transaction is the only place that knows what was decided, the same on every node. Three values with three readers (anchor, version, coverage), three write outcomes (`applied` / `pending` / `unknown`, never a bool) — and TWO PENDINGS, told apart by `Waited`: one waited and the node is behind, one never asked, and reported as a single fact a deliberate skip reads to an operator as a node falling behind under load. `NoWait` has exactly ONE correct caller, which holds its answer without the rows: a sign-in's session record, because the cookie carries the record's own position and every node that serves the API — a data node — validates against its own applier, so the row this node would wait for is a row nothing in the answer reads; it does NOT touch the session wait, which is the one that makes a decision read the caller's own previous write, and the FLOOR THEOREM in the package doc with all three of its enforced preconditions, because retry-at-zero on a trimmed anchor is safe only because of them and any consumer using per-subject conditional append inherits the hazard. AN OPERATION ID CARRIES THE INSTANT IT WAS MINTED — `<uuidv7>[.<name>][.<step>…]`, minted only by `NewOpID`, `DeriveOpID` (an id a retry must reproduce, at the start of its unit of work) or `StepOpID` (one append of a gesture), and held by `CheckCallerOpID` where a caller brings one back — because THE LEDGER ANSWERS FIRST: an operation already in it is `Collapsed` and its decide never runs, so a caller builds on nothing that decide would have filled; the ledger TRAVELS in every snapshot (`Divergent`) beside a watermark of how far back it may have lost rows, per table and per subject KIND (`Rows.LostBefore`, `statelog_ops_lost_kind`), so the identity estate's hourly session sweep leaves every other kind vouched for over the month; and an operation minted before the watermark with no row is `unknown` and `Unvouched` — ask another node — rather than decided twice. AN ID'S NAME AND EVERY STEP ARE ONE SEGMENT each — visible ASCII with no dot, at most `MaxOpSegmentBytes` (91, what the 128-byte bound on a caller's id leaves after the uuid and its dot) and not beginning with `~` — and the three minters write anything else ESCAPED, as `~` and 128 bits of its SHA-256 in hex, deterministic so a derived id still reproduces and injective since a segment written as itself never begins with `~`, because written as handed a file path or a dotted node id became steps of another operation in an id the engine's own caller rule refuses; `OpNamed` compares through the same rule, a keyed write's verb must be a segment as written since a reader finds the operation by it, a value composed into a segment goes through `OpNamePart` (64 bytes) so the verb beside it stays readable, and the dashboard's gate minter carries the same escape over a SHA-256 of its own, held to the engine's by `testdata/opname_vectors.json`. Every record is STAMPED with its writer's node and generation (`Request.Decide(tx, Stamp)`) and is a SIGNED FRAME (ADR-0031: the frame, the keyring, the signer, the verifier and the three verdicts are the leaf `recordseal`'s, and what is the state log's is that its appender seals every record and its readers open every one before a domain decodes it, `signature.go`), so a reader that decodes straight off the log rather than through an applier is handed a `VerifiedReader` (a `VerifiedLog` over the log and the keyring's verifier), and a raw log does not compile there. Every identity-claiming log carries NODE GATES (`Domain.NodeGate`, `EvictionProbe`, `Evictions`), GENERATION RECORDS of its own for a per-log reanchor (`GenerationEncoder`), and a GATE RESERVE at the top of its ceiling that ordinary writes are refused `log_full` short of and an eviction or a readmission lands in, so the gesture that unpins a full log is not refused by the fullness it exists to clear — the larger of a sixteenth of the ceiling and the FLEET TERM, seven peers' largest appends and a mebibyte, because what the reserve absorbs is what peers hold in flight and that is a property of the LOG: every domain DECLARES its largest record (`StreamSpec.MaxRecordBytes`), the publisher refuses a record past it and the stream's `max_msg_size` holds a peer on another build to it, so the identity estate's (128 KiB) is sized by its own records rather than by the transport's 8 MiB, which a sixteenth of its 64 MiB floor could not hold even one of. A usage the admission cannot read refuses the write `usage_unknown` before its append, typed in `Reserve.Admit` (the one place that knows nothing was appended), retryable, and a refusal about THIS node that Gitlet hands to the repository's runner-up. A RECORD IS STAMPED WITH THE LOWEST VERSION ITS FIELDS NEED, never the build's: every domain declares the fields its records gained since the base format and the version each arrived at (`RecordFields`, one table per domain, which `statelogtest` certifies), because stamped below what its fields need an older node decodes the record, drops what it has no home for and applies the rest — its rows then differ from every upgraded node's for good, with nothing to report it — and stamped at the build's version every write the new build makes, the ones carrying nothing new included, is retained on every older node for the length of a rolling upgrade. A GATE record is the one an older node does not retain — it STOPS on one above the version it reads, because deferring an eviction would go on applying everything the evicted node appends — so a field a gate's record gains is marked as one (`VersionedField.Gate`), the gates stay at `GateRecordVersion` until it lands, and its writer waits for the fleet's census of read versions (below) before publishing one. One suite certifies every domain — `statelogtest`, in the `queuetest`/`coordtest` idiom, with a control expected to come back clean and a meta-test that hands it a domain which lies. A STREAM'S IDENTITY is the creation instant the create that made it STAMPED into its configuration (`statelog.CreatedAtKey`, `crewlet.created_at`), read by every consumer through `StreamCreatedAt` — never the broker's own, which a snapshot restore resets to the restore: read off the broker, every log a node restored from a backup held was "recreated", and the node served nothing. ADR-0083, and `TestOnlyStreamCreatedAtReadsAStreamsCreationInstant` holds it: no other non-test file selects `Created` on a stream's information, typed by `sourcetree/decltype`'s walk of the declarations — generics included — with a read it cannot type reported rather than passed. Its ALARM TABLE lives here rather than beside any one subsystem, because an alarm is the framework's answer to "is this node doing its job" and everything above it asks the same question. Every alarm fires at a threshold ANOTHER decision already made — the grace that takes a copy out of service, the grace that stops a node serving a copy it cannot decode, the budget a caller was promised, the replay window an operator set a log's ceiling to hold, the most live refs a push decide lets a repository hold and the window after which the ref lifecycle deletes a seat's idle branch (`code_refs_near_limit`, whose reader judges each repository at both) — because an alarm with a threshold of its own is a second opinion about one event, and the two drift. One evaluation feeds every surface, so a gauge, a log line and a screen can never disagree about whether something is wrong. A COPY of a database holds its write-ahead log for its whole run, and two alarms read that: `wal_large` names the copy holding the largest log (`Reading.WALCopy`, from `store.DB.Copies`) — a backup's or a donor snapshot's, whose end folds the log back in — rather than reading it as a reader holding a snapshot open, and `volume_low` keeps room beside the second copy for the log the next one holds back (`Reading.CopyHeldBytes`, from `store.DB.CopyHoldsBack`). Three of its inputs are MEASURED rather than read off a gauge: a strict log's intake over the trailing day, counted out of the log's own records (every record of the day is still in it, `min_age` being floored at a day) and a POINTER in the reading, because a log that took in nothing and a log nobody measured — compacted, younger than the day, a node that has not ticked — are opposite facts; how many records a BLOCKED TRIM is keeping past `min_age`, the published age term against the log's first record, because every young fleet's trim is blocked (a first backup, first donors, a log nobody writes to) and only a trim blocked for longer than the window and a tick (`TrimInterval`, declared beside the arithmetic because it is the block's resolution) while its log keeps something past the window is `trim_blocked`; and how long the trim floor has been UNREADABLE, an age this node's own evaluations observed from first sighting to latest, because no record carries when it began — a health read has no memory, and an alarm fed one could only say "unknown now" and stood its own threshold in for the age. A fourth is measured by the engine's position heartbeat and handed in with the bound it is judged against: `clock_skew`, this node's clock and the clock of the broker member leading the position register, each against the FLEET'S clock — the median of the data nodes' clocks, read off the register's rows, each the instant its node stamped against the instant the store took it (`coord.NodePositions.StoredAt`) — so the alarm names the clock that moved, where measured against the member alone it blamed every node for the member's drift and let the member, a data node on an embedded broker, read nothing; each judged against `objstore.AssumedClockSkew`, the hour the object collector's grace and Gitlet's retired-pack sweep both rest on, which the reading carries because this framework imports neither the object store nor Gitlet (ADR-0015). A deferral's age is the position heartbeat's first sighting read through `DeferredSince.Age`, the one arithmetic the copy's judgement and `deferred_old` both take, so the instant the alarm names is the instant the copy goes out of service — and a held record and an unreadable floor are evaluated PER LOG, like the headroom, the ceiling, the blocked trim and the census, because what the grace does and which re-anchor a floor needs are the log's: one alarm naming a node's oldest record said an identity record took nothing out of service while a younger tracker record had taken the copy out. What is per log is the EVALUATION and the LOG LINE, never the alarm: an alarm is ONE PER KIND and lists every log it stands on in `Alarm.Domains`, each with its own measurement (and, for a held trim, the term holding it and since when), its detail the most pressing log's — and a log the backup term holds past its replay window while `backup_age` fires is listed under `backup_age` rather than raising a `trim_blocked` of its own, since the backup is its remedy (a younger hold is listed under neither) — because raised once per log, one missing backup and four held logs read as five alarms on the health count while the gauge said two, and the screen drew one cause as five problems; so the count, the report, the gauge (one series per kind), the dashboard, the presence heartbeat and `crewlet retention status` say one cause once. The TRACKER still writes its lines per (kind, log), forming an instance from each alarm's `Domains`: a second log joining a kind already up writes its own `alarm_raised` and a log leaving it its own `alarm_cleared` with its own start, because keyed on the kind alone it folded the second log into the first — no line when it started, none when the first cleared, and one final clear carrying the last log's detail against the first one's start. What it holds as standing is ONE computation behind both `Standing` (the health envelope's count and `worst`) and `Marks` (each kind with the instant its oldest instance was raised, which the presence heartbeat carries as `coord.NodeStatus.Alarms`), so a node's health card and the fleet view cannot name a different set or a different longest-standing alarm. A node-wide kind is one instance, `backup_age` included, whatever logs it lists. Each instance's onset and clearing is also HANDED ON, once, to whoever the node asked to be told (`Tracker.OnTransition`, called under the tracker's lock so two racing evaluations hand theirs on in order): an `AlarmTransition` whose id `TransitionID` derives from the node, the kind, the log, the change and the instant the instance was raised, and the first evaluation's finds `firing_at_boot` rather than `fired`, since the tracker cannot tell an alarm that started then from one that stood through a restart — which is also how a clear its node did not live to hand on is answered. That transition IS the record the granted seats' wakes derive from (ADR-0095), never a record on a log: the alarms most worth a wake are about the logs, and a log at its ceiling would refuse it. `Describe` hands a surface away from the reference the table's own meaning and remedy for a kind. THREE LOOPS PER DATA NODE make its recovery path real rather than declared, and each is useless without the other two: a POSITION HEARTBEAT (the trim takes a minimum across these rows, so a node that publishes nothing is one it cannot see and trims past — and each row names the record version the node's build reads on each log, which a successor's writer of a record this build cannot even DEFER — a gate above the version it reads — waits on through `statelog.Readers` over the same counted set; nothing this build writes needs it, since no gate record it writes is above the base format — the one record above it, the usage log's `repo_read` at version 2, is one an older node DEFERS), a SNAPSHOTTER (one artefact series per data node, of the replicated estate it keeps whole from boot — taken and offered whether or not the node may WRITE: a barred machine back with its files writes nothing and may hold the fleet's only copy, and held to the write rule its joiner had no donor — declining while it is catching up, holds an undecodable record, is short of disk — for the copy, a tenth beside it and the write-ahead log the copy holds back while it runs, which `store.DB.CopyHoldsBack` measures, on the snapshots' volume, and for that log on the live file's own — or the trim counts no OTHER node on the estate's logs — and retrying soon rather than waiting out the interval, because every one of those clears at boot), and a DONOR (every data node offers its newest artefact, because a fleet whose only donor was down would have nothing to give). The recipient half alone is the worst state this has: it reports itself working while asking a fleet that can never answer. A FOURTH loop is the TRIM, and it is the one without which a log only grows: a fleet singleton (`retention`) evaluating six terms per log over the log's counted set — every live data node, and a listing that cannot be read publishing the floor BLOCKED rather than skipping the tick — purging what all six permit, and PUBLISHING what it concluded — because which term came lowest is one tick's conclusion and HOW LONG it has been lowest is a property of a series of them, and a duty that moves on a lease carries no memory across the move. A stream's CEILING is the one setting none of that can change while the engine is running: a resize is decided against the usage the log is at and a publisher makes that a moving quantity, and what retires a request the broker already queued is the broker PROCESS restarting. So it is a fleet-wide window across three modes — `normal` publishes, `maintenance` may write configuration, `seal` may NOT, which is precisely what makes a seal-mode acknowledgement evidence rather than a claim — driven by an evidence table (`maintenance.go`) that states every transition once. Two of its inputs have no other source: a backup ANNOUNCES what it covers when its manifest is written (the node holding the duty is rarely the node that took the copy and can never see a directory on another host), and the evictions come from the REPLICATED rows rather than a bucket, because that is where an eviction actually lives. SETTLED IS NOT APPLIED: the checkpoint moves past a record a node RETAINS, so a reader that decides from an ABSENT row reads `PrefixIn` — the prefix its own snapshot has APPLIED — and `DeferredIn` — whether any retained record's scope covers what it reads, asked of the whole deferral index and never the earliest record — inside the transaction that reads the rows; and an applier whose listeners hold a decision made before such a commit implements the optional `RetentionHook`, told after the commit and immediately before `Committed` how many records the batch retained, because a retained record never reaches Apply and so moved nothing an applier could have gathered. A CALLER'S FLOORS ARE ONE PER LOG (`Freshness.Floors`, checked where a wire names them by `ValidFloors`: one per log, at most `MaxFloors`, four, twice the widest answer composed), because one answer can be read from two logs and its caller may have written to both: a read of several logs hands each half the floor on its own log (`Freshness.On`: a COPY of the whole ask with only its floors narrowed, never a literal naming the parts it keeps, which would drop a part added later without a word, and a `session` half its caller named no floor on read at `stale` rather than under the stronger name), a reader of one log refuses a floor on any other as the request's mistake (`Query.Floors`, `Freshness.OnlyOn`, `ErrForeignPosition`) rather than waiting on its own and dropping the rest, and a composed answer reports the weakest level a half was read at (`Weakest`) The MODEL ALARMS are per ENTRY (`perEntry`, `Alarm.Entries`), the analogue of per-log: five `llm_*` kinds at the owner's fixed thresholds (30 days, 7 days, 15 minutes), with no setting; `Tracker.Latest` is what the Models page reads, so it cannot disagree with the health count. |
| `textindex` | The engine's own lexical search: the analyzer that turns a document into terms, and the BM25 arithmetic over the inverted list they are stored in. It exists because Turso has NO fts5 and no `fts` index method — `internal/store/caps.go` measures both once per process and reports them on every open, and behind the experimental flag that gates every `USING` clause the engine answers `unknown module name 'fts'`, so the gate is not what is missing, and the alternatives were refusing knowledge search on the only driver this build ships or embedding a search library with its own index format, file and backup story on every data node. PURE FUNCTIONS OVER VALUES — the SQL is `search`'s — so the ranking is testable without a database and an index rebuild cannot quietly change it. The BM25 tuning is a named PROFILE rather than two package-level numbers, because a knowledge base and a chat want opposite length normalisations from one arithmetic. K1 is 1.2 on BOTH — these documents repeat their subject constantly and a higher one ranks by verbosity instead of by coverage, and a person who says a word twice in a message means it as much as a page that says it twice — while B splits: `ProseProfile` at 0.75 for pages and work items, `ChatProfile` at 0.30 because a chat corpus is bimodal — one-line acknowledgements beside pasted blocks — and the prose tuning hands every query to whoever typed the shortest reply. A test pins each by the BEHAVIOUR it buys rather than by its value, and the zero profile scores nothing rather than ranking by a tuning nobody chose. A `Reading` says how a text the index does not hold is read — `Plain`, as written, or `JSON`, through the escapes a JSON text's strings are written in, as a JSON decoder reads them, so `"cd repo\ngit push"` holds `git` and not `ngit`; only a text that is JSON, since a Windows path's `\new` read so loses its `n` — and only which character each byte is: a word is a run of letters and digits however a text is read. `Reading.Find` answers whether a text holds every term of a query and where the earliest begins, through THE SAME TOKENIZER the index and the query side run — a whole term, never a substring — streaming, with no allocation per word, and stopping once every term is seen: what a search of one text, such as a transcript's entry, decides by, so it finds what a search through the index would; `Reading.FindIn` asks it of a text handed over in pieces, each at its offset and no term read across two — a redacted text's own words between its markers — without a copy of the text with the gaps blanked. `Reading.MayHold` says of a text whether stretches cut from it could hold every term at all — each inside one of its words, whole or as a piece, since a stretch can cut a word short and never make one up; and read as JSON, inside a word a stretch begun inside an escape reads too, the escape's body as written or the escape a `\\`'s second backslash opens, and the word after it, so that a stretch's own reading never finds what MayHold of the whole text says it may not — what a caller asks before it pays to cut them, and it decides nothing: asked `Find` of the text whole instead, a term a redaction's marker ended short was missed unless the text held it whole somewhere else, under the redaction, and found where it did. `Snippet` centres a hit's window on the first WHOLE term `Plain.Find` finds, as a lexical search decided the hit, never on a longer word that merely holds the term's letters where the body holds the term whole — and where it holds none whole, as a hybrid search's candidate only its semantic ranker found often does (no stemming: "Deployments" for "deploy"), on the first word holding one, never on the preamble; `SnippetFrom` centres it on the word its caller finds in the body as the window is cut from it, for a caller that decided its hit on less than every word of the body — a redaction's own words — so the snippet shows the word the hit was found by and not the same letters in a marker before it. |
