An INTERDIFF (`interdiff.go`) is a diff read of two revisions' heads whose stat and patch are KEPT to the exact SET of either revision's touched paths (`pathFilter` — `a*` a file's name, never a pathspec, which a diff would take on its command line alone, with no --pathspec-from-file), WALKING NEITHER HEAD: each touched path is LOOKED UP at both heads by ONE `cat-file --batch-check=%(objectmode) %(objectname) %(objecttype) -Z` fed `<head>:<path>` lines (`touchedRecords`), and the raw record diff-tree would write is made here for each path whose entries differ (a tree is no entry, a change of type `T`), in git's order of full paths, for diff-pairs to count or patch — so its git is O(touched), at most 2 × `code.MaxTouchedPaths` lookups, never the target's churn between the two bases, which a walk of the heads read whole — and by none where either touches all or the two share a base, since their heads then differ only in files one touches — answered and memoized as a diff is (Kind interdiff). EVERY PAGE A RUN CUTS IS MEMOIZED in the copy's memo (`memo.go`, the cache's `Memo`), keyed by the format, the page bound, the kind, every whole id, the normalised arguments and the cursor: a read naming whole ids asks it as soon as the grant is judged and BEFORE ANY GIT RUNS — the presence check would leave a hit no faster than two processes, and the memo is the copy's, so an entry exists only where this copy found its objects — and one naming an abbreviation once it is expanded; a hit holds no share unit and is stamped (position, pushes, coverage, `Memo`) as a cut page is. git cannot seek inside an object or a listing, so the run that misses cuts EVERY PAGE from the asked one to its answer's end (a listing, a file's range, a stat's files — each page's counts written into its staged entry once the stat has counted past it, `pageCounts`, so a run holds one page's counts and never every file's — and a patch), each the page a read from its cursor cuts — `blobPages` and `patchPages` chain the one-page cutters at the next cursor — so a file read page by page streams once, inside the read's one budget of git; a comparison is one page, a landed-in read, a revision's facts (asked once a revision and a target by whoever records them, and an id omitted for time is no page to keep) and a re-anchoring (keyed by a list of anchors each caller makes anew) never memoized. A miss of a page another read of the node is cutting is a SINGLE FLIGHT (`read.await`, keyed by the repository and the page's memo key): it waits for that read to answer — holding no share unit and no read-lane slot, its own answer's deadline bounding the wait — and is answered from the memo it filled, so N seats asking one page at once run one git; one whose memo still misses runs its own, unled. A page carries its BUDGET, the most its stamps may cost and it still fit, so one whose stamps grew is cut again; pages are encoded BINARY (varints, strings sliced from one copy), since encoding/json would decode a 400-entry page at a few tens of MB/s, and `memoFormat` is pinned to a fingerprint of the answer types (`TestAnAnswersShapeIsItsMemoFormat`). A read asked UNSTAMPED (`code.GitQuery.Unstamped`, a page's kinds only) reads no index of pushes and is stamped with nothing — no repository, position, memo, push or coverage (`read.stamp`, the one place they are set, which the envelope a page is cut against and a memoized page's budget read too) — so its page is cut against a room no stamp moves and is a function of the object ids it names, its arguments and the build alone: what a question answers immutable; it is memoized under a key of its own, since the stamped cut of the same read is another page. Asked of the repository's HOME Gitlet node first by the estate's walk, and built by the engine beside Gitlet over the same cache and pool (`native.gitReads`). Holds no goroutine, and is STOPPED by whoever stops Gitlet, before its cache (`Server.Stop`): every read after it is answered unready, `node_failed`, starting nothing, and every read in flight is CUT — the server's own lifetime ends every read's context — answered the same while its asker listens, and waited for, so once the stop returns no read of the node is being answered or recorded; the host never counted these reads among its requests, so a read in flight outlived its stop. A read of a `visibility: unit` repository that answered, a memo hit included, is recorded (`Options.Fetched`, required: one read via `tool`, with its kind, the asker and the answer's encoded size, filed by the engine in the node's reads ledger, `code/readaudit`, so neither the read nor one waiting on the page it cuts waits on the broker for its record). A SEAT'S SECOND LOOK AT THE LOG'S HEAD IS ITS TURN'S TO PAY (`Options.Resyncs`, `code.NewResyncs`, ONE a node with Gitlet's boxes and engine writes): its turn (`code.GitQuery.Turn`, stamped by the builtins' one `gitRead`) on its seat, 16 refilled at the census's 125 a seat-day, and past it the refusal is answered from the copy at the seat's floor, saying `(not re-judged at linearizable: …)`; a read made for a check (`/box/gitlet/`) pays its attempt's bucket on its repository's checks (`code.CheckKey.Resyncs`) — the one its git pays to Gitlet on that node, so an attempt has one burst a node, counted `crewlet.code.box.resyncs` with its git's; a person's and the engine's own reads are never charged. A SEARCH (`search.go`, `code.GitSearch`, M6-D12/D13) names a REF, not an id — CONTINUED AFTER A PLACE (`code.SearchQuery.After`), it reads no file whose path sorts before the place's and drops every line at or before it before its limit counts one, the place a part of its memo key — and it resolves its commit (`rev-parse --verify`, looked for once more at the log's head) before the memo is asked, then reads it ONE OF TWO WAYS that answer the same lines, RE2's, in path and line order — THROUGH THE CODE INDEX where the copy's (`cache.Cache.IndexTip`, `CodeIndex`) answers for that commit (the plan's candidates in every segment, kept where the tip map names them at a path the query's filter admits, read through one `cat-file --batch` in path order, confirmed line by line), and otherwise WITH `git grep -I -n -z -E` over `codeindex.Plan.Grep`'s ONE alternation of escaped strings (one pattern, never one a string: git's look-ahead rescans the rest of a file for each pattern after every hit), every line it answers confirmed the same way and every file past `code.MaxIndexedFileBytes` dropped by its `ls-tree -l` size as the index skips it — the query's paths filtered HERE over git's answer, never handed to git as a pathspec. The search's git runs under ONE unit of the share within the read's budget of git, and the whole within `code.SearchBudget` (5 s, the resolve budget): one that runs it out answers what it found, `Truncated`, and is memoized NOWHERE, its page no function of its arguments; a complete one is memoized under the commit, the ref and every part of the query, whichever path cut it. At most `code.MaxSearchHits` (500) lines of `code.MaxSearchLineBytes` (256) each. The FIRST of an indexed repository's two index holders, asked as its walk's home, whose index does not answer for the default branch's tip yet, answers `index_building` (no fill passed) so the second holder answers; no other node refuses so (`cache.IndexedTip.PassesOn`), so a walk always ends at an answer. |
| `code/readaudit` | WHO READ A UNIT'S REPOSITORY, AS THE NODE THAT SERVED THE READS KEEPS THEM BETWEEN FLUSHES: every clone and fetch Gitlet served and every server-side read the git reads answered of a `visibility: unit` repository, FILED as it is answered (`Ledger.Add`, a fold under one lock) and published every 15 s as ONE `code_fetched` record per key — company day, repository, principal kind and principal, way, a server-side read's kind, and the seat it acted as — counting its reads and summing their bytes, named as its newest read named the repository and stamped with that read's instant, so a record never straddles a company day and a CI token fetching every few seconds is a record a flush, not one a fetch. A `coalesce` ledger, so OFF THE READ'S PATH: a read used to be published as it was answered, and while the event stream had no leader each held its fetch's response, or its slot on the git lane, up to the client's five seconds — sixty-four of them the whole lane, every repository's reads queued behind them — and a refused publish lost its record for good; now a refused record waits sealed for the next flush, up to `coalesce.MaxPending`. Built ONCE on the engine (`codeReads`), not with Gitlet, since the host is rebuilt at an apply; its last flush is the teardown's, at once with the auxiliary spend's, after Gitlet stops and before the usage publisher's own |
| `codeindex` | GITLET'S TRIGRAM INDEX AS PURE FUNCTIONS OVER BYTES — which three-byte runs each blob holds, the two files a repository's index is kept in (a SEGMENT, `CRCX`: a blob table with an escape and a skipped flag, a trigram table, uvarint postings; a TIP MAP, `CRCT`: a tip's every path and the blob at it; each under a SHA-256 trailer, the cache's run-trailer check), the PLAN of a regular expression over them, and the QUERY a person or a seat writes — so a code search reads only the few files that can match. It reads and writes no file and runs no git: the cache owns the files, `code/query` the git. Postings are keyed by BLOB, never by path or commit, so a new tip indexes only the blobs it introduced, a compaction or a re-clone changes nothing here, and which postings count is the tip map's to say; a merge (`MergeSegments`) keeps only what its keep keeps, writing the very bytes a build of those blobs writes, and merges each trigram's lists IN PAIRS between two buffers kept from trigram to trigram — as a plan unions a clause's literals —, so its work is L·⌈log₂ k⌉ and it allocates nothing a posting, where folding the lists in one at a time cost k·L and allocated 69 bytes a posting over 32 segments. Trigrams are taken over the blob's UNICODE LOWERING (`bytes.ToLower`), the comparison `regexlit`'s prefilter makes for a folded literal — an ASCII-only lowering is cheaper and misses `(?i)` across É and é — and a blob holding an escape (`regexlit.HasEscape`, ſ) carries a flag every clause holding a folded literal admits, since no lowering sees through it. Both are taken with the Unicode tables the build carries, which move with the Go toolchain and give letters a case they lacked, while a segment outlives its build (kept across restarts, hard-linked across incarnations, never re-read for a blob it holds) — so a segment is STAMPED with `unicode.Version` and a build carrying other tables refuses it as `ErrMalformed`, which rebuilds the index rather than ruling out a blob a newer lowering looks up by other bytes; a tip map holds nothing the tables decide and is not stamped. The plan is `regexlit.Required`'s clauses, looked up where every literal of a clause is three bytes or more lowered; a plan is looked up reading each posting list it names ONCE, whichever literals of whichever clauses hold the trigram (`lookup.go`) — the blobs holding what every literal of a clause holds read once for all of them, each literal admitting only blobs among those; a list more than one place reads, of one clause or of several, decoded once for them all, as far as the furthest blob one needs; a list one place reads, read there alone, into nothing, as far as what it keeps reaches — and a clause another implies is not looked up at all (a part a pattern repeats is a clause each time to `regexlit.Required`: `(foo.*){100}` was a hundred lookups of foo, each holding its every blob) — where looking a literal up at a time read a list once for every literal holding it and decoded it into a buffer of its own each time (a clause of 64 words sharing lists over 2 048 blobs: 289 280 bytes of postings read and 1 457 152 allocated, against 12 288 and 100 288); a pattern with no such clause is REFUSED (`ErrNoLiteral`) rather than answered by reading every file, as is one that can match across a line (`ErrNotLineLocal`); candidates are CONFIRMED by Go's regexp line by line, so the index and the grep path both answer RE2, never a second dialect. What a confirm may cost is BOUNDED where the plan is made, because Go's regexp may step every instruction of its program at every byte and a run of it cannot be stopped part way: a pattern whose program is past `MaxProgram` (1 024 instructions) is REFUSED (`ErrTooComplex`) — 400 bytes of counted repetitions compile to a hundred thousand, 1.5–2 ms a byte of a line —, `Confirm` runs the expression on a line only where its bytes times the program's instructions are within `MaxLineWork` (2^25: 0.22 s at the measured 6.7 ns an instruction-byte, and a short program still reads a whole minified line), counting a longer line that could match rather than running it or calling it a miss, and checks its caller's context between lines, so a search's budget holds to within one line's run. A blob past `MaxFileBytes` (1 MiB) or binary by git's own test (`Binary`: a NUL in the first 8 000 bytes, the rule `git grep -I` falls back to — the ONE copy of it, which `code/query`'s file reads call too) is SKIPPED: recorded so no later tip reads it again, and never a candidate. `ParseQuery` reads leading `repo:`, `path:` and `ref:` filters, then the text as written, at most `MaxQueryBytes` (400: knowledge search's bound, held to it by a test, since the knowledge seam is not pure); every mode (literal, regex, word) is an RE2 expression under `(?m)`; a path filter reads as a `.gitignore` line without negation, escapes or classes. Its suite writes patterns over non-ASCII case orbits and the long s, and blobs matching them from each pattern's own syntax tree (`regexlit/regexlittest`), and holds that no blob Go's regexp matches is ever ruled out. `Plan.Grep` is the GREP PATH'S HALF of the same plan: the strings of the most selective clause git reads EXACTLY, as ONE `git grep -E` alternation with every byte of its syntax escaped — never a string a `-F` pattern, whose look-ahead rescans the rest of a file for each pattern after every hit, nor the query's own expression, a second dialect; never a clause with a string holding a NUL or a newline; one with no folded literal outside ASCII, since git's `-i` folds ASCII alone and lowers no line — and, where it folds, every rune outside ASCII that RE2's `(?i)` folds onto an ASCII letter or whose lowering is one, since a folded literal is held as its lowering (the long s, the Kelvin sign, İ, derived from the Unicode tables), so the lines git answers are a superset of RE2's and a repository read with git grep answers what the index would; a plan with no such clause has git answer every line |
| `codesearch` | A CODE SEARCH OF EVERY REPOSITORY AN ASKER MAY READ, on the Gitlet nodes that hold them (M6-D14). ONE repository is a git read of it (`code.GitSearch`) through the keyed walk, whose answer or refusal is the search's. MORE are ONE SCATTER on `topics.CodeSearch`, never a walk a repository — an unfiltered search of a company would be thousands of requests: every Gitlet node serves it, and the request carries an ASSIGNMENT TABLE, each repository named under the first node of its git order (`estate.Router.GitOrders`, one reading for the whole table: its home, and for an indexed repository the first index holder), because every server of a subject hears every request and a scatter divides work by what it names; a repository its node did not answer is asked ONCE more of the next node of its order (the second index holder) and never a third time, so a search's wait is two rounds of `RoundBudget` at most (9 s: the share wait, the search's own 5 s and a reply margin each way — a sum of whole budgets — and a round ends once every node asked has answered). A serving node searches each repository through `code/query` AS THE ASKER THE REQUEST NAMES, its grant judged from that node's own chart, each repository's one second look at the log's head synced to the head the asker's linearizable listing read (`Request.Head`, `code.GitQuery.Head`) rather than a barrier a repository — so the request is an INSTRUCTION and the scatter a `signedask.Channel` (`code.search`): unsigned, any broker client could read any repository as anybody; a request the fleet did not sign, a replay and one past its deadline answer nothing, one under a key the node does not hold answers `Unverified`. A node's searches TOGETHER read at most `ScatterReads(units)` of its repositories at once — ALL BUT ONE unit of its seat git-work share (`code.GitShare.Units`), one where it has one — across every request it answers: each read's search takes a unit of that share FIFO behind every seat's read, and bounded by the answer slots instead (64 a request, 64 requests a node) one unfiltered search queued 64 waiters on every node's share and pushed every seat's reads past `GitShareWait`; a read past its answer's due waiting for a slot is `UnreadyShare`, and its runner-up is asked. THE MERGE IS EXACT: every repository answers its first lines by path bytes and line, a node keeps the first `Limit` of its repositories' lines by (name, path, line), the asker the first `Limit` of every node's — no line a node left out can precede one another kept, and a round assigns a repository to one node, so the answer is the same whichever node answers first — and the asker keeps no line past the last of a repository that STOPPED EARLY (its answer's bound or its budget: `prefixEnd`), so every line before the answer's last is in it. A MERGE HOLDS THE LIMIT, NEVER THE ANSWERS: each answer is folded in and cut as it arrives, so a node holds `Limit` lines and its reads in flight however many repositories it is assigned — never every answer until the last (a gigabyte at five thousand repositories and `Limit` 500); and a node reads its repositories in NAME ORDER and passes over, unread, one its first `Limit` lines all precede — a common word reads the repositories that fill the limit, not the company — every repository named after the last line kept being `PastLimit` by its name alone, so the coverage does not turn on how reads interleaved. A PAGE CONTINUES AFTER ITS `Key` (`Query.After`: repository, commit, path, line): no repository before the key's is asked, the key's own is read at the key's commit past its line (`code.SearchQuery.After`, which `code/query` honours by reading no file before the path and dropping lines before the limit counts them), so a page costs the lines from its place on and a push between pages repeats or skips no line. EVERY ANSWER SAYS WHAT IT DID NOT SEARCH (`Coverage`): each repository named is in exactly one of — by what the LAST node asked for it answered, so a silent runner-up is `NotAnswering` — searched, `Building` (the index holder building, its order naming no runner-up), `Stale` (a node behind the log or the configuration), `NotAnswering` (by node, with why), `NotPermitted` (a chart that moved since the listing), `NoRef` and `PastLimit`, beside `GrepNotNamed` (the grep repositories an unfiltered search leaves out — grep runs only on those `repo:` names, at most `MaxGrepRepos`, 8, a monorepo's grep being a CPU-second or two; a filter's names are read BESIDE EACH OTHER, `ResolveReads` (9) at once, so their linearizable row reads join one barrier a wave rather than one a name, and a filter past the grep bound is refused as the rows arrive, the rest unread) and `NotIndexed` (indexed ones read with grep), each a count and its first names in order — the names of every set and every node's reason sharing ONE budget, `MaxCoverageText` (4 KiB, a sixteenth of a seat's tool answer, the reasons in at most half and each at most `MaxGapWhyBytes`), every count whole: a cap a set (100 names) was three quarters of an answer at real name lengths, `NotAnswering`'s sets growing with the fleet beside it. The text is bounded as knowledge search's (`codeindex.MaxQueryBytes`, 400, refused and never cut) before anything is listed. Counted as `crewlet.code.search.queries{via}`, `.duration{via}` and `.coverage{reason}`. A refusal over ONE repository — a `repo:` naming one nobody declared or the asker may not read, or the one repository a search reads refusing it — is a `RepoRefusal` naming it, so a surface answering it (`code_search`'s `not_declared`) says which |
| `learning` | What a seat remembers. Everything here is BEST EFFORT by design: a failed write is logged, a failed read answers empty. `memsync` is the exception that makes the rest true across a fleet: a seat's memory is written to the NODE's store, and placement moves seats — so every memory row rides a COMPACTED CHANGELOG (one subject per row, one message retained per subject) and a node hydrates a seat's rows before its mailbox attaches — READING TO WHERE THE CHANGELOG'S LEADER SAYS THEY END (`jsapi.Leader` over the seat's wildcard, a `STREAM.MSG.GET` whatever the stream's allow_direct says, asked again while nobody answers), because the replay is a consumer the server places on any replica, and one hosted on a copy behind an acknowledged write stopped short of the seat's newest rows and reported success. Deletes deliberately do not travel: the lifecycle re-converges, and a tombstone protocol would be a second thing to keep correct forever. It DECLARES the two `statelog` contracts it rests on rather than implementing their shapes privately: `ReplayCompacted`, which every rule in the hydration follows from, and STREAM IDENTITY — because a recreated changelog is EMPTY, so hydrating from one reports success and gives every seat on the node a blank diary, and a compacted stream has no checkpoint and no generation to answer a recreation with, so its only honest move is to refuse the seat. A SEAT'S MEMORY IS KEYED ON ITS HANDLE, which is immutable (ADR-0013): the diary and onboarding markers on the agent id derived from it, and episodes, both skill tables, counterparty profiles (a colleague subject included) on the handle itself, in the `agent_handle`/`observer_handle`/`subject_handle` columns memsync carries rows between peers by. `memread` is the other half: every node that ever ran a seat keeps a copy and only the HOLDER's is current, so a screen's read of a seat's memory follows the seat's LEASE — answered here, asked of the holding incarnation on an ephemeral scatter every node serves (a node serving no API may be the holder), or empty and naming nobody for a seat no node holds — and a silent or still-hydrating holder is `unavailable`, never an empty memory. A read names its seat both ways (`memread.Seat`): the agent id its lease, diary and onboarding marker are keyed by, and the handle the rest of its memory is keyed by. A screen's read of a seat's skills carries its ORDER (`skills_order`: `newest`, the zero value, `uses` or `updated`, `learning.SkillOrders`, each ending on the id) and the HOLDER orders the whole set before it cuts the page — an additive field within the wire's version 1 — because a page sorted after it was cut answers "the most used of the newest fifty"; the dashboard's `LEARNED_SKILL_ORDERS` is held to the list by a `clientsource` row. Its reads RAISE, unlike the turn's: "remembers nothing" and "the store did not answer" are opposite facts on a screen. And the WRITE side follows the seat for the same reason: post-turn reflection is fed by a `reflection_due` wake on the SEAT'S OWN subject, attached by the holder after hydration and let go before the release's last flush — on one fleet-wide group, all but one in N of a seat's reflections wrote memory where nothing carried or read it. A seat's PAST ASK keeps WHO WROTE IT: an episode stores the `provenance.Label` its turn's ask was read under (`ask_provenance`, node migration 0058, carried by memsync with the ask), and `RenderPastTurn` is the ONE rendering of a past turn into a model's text — the ask fenced under that label, everything else on the line neutralised — because a stranger's message recalled a month on is not the seat's own memory, which is the voice it trusts most; a label that does not decode reads as the zero label, fenced and vouched for by nobody, never as none. And the POST-TURN WORKERS that write that memory (the persist decider, the profiler, the skill synthesizer and refiner) read what the turn was told FENCED as the turn read it — each inbound message under its own label through ONE rendering (`inboundBody`), the ask under the turn's record of it (`describeTurn`), under a token minted per call beside the standing sentence their system prompts end on — and everything else they are shown neutralised, because what they write the seat reads later as its own |
| `schedule` | Role- and unit-scoped cron work, with at-most-once delivery, missed-tick catchup and a wall-clock cap. A restart records its most recent fire as MISSED ONLY WHEN NOBODY HOLDS ITS MINUTE (`Claimer.MinuteClaimed`, answered by the fleet): claiming the runner-less skip cannot say so, because it collides with no runner's fire, and the node's own ledger cannot either, because a moved duty does not carry it. A fire older than the claim retention is not judged at all. EACH SCHEDULE IS A CONVERSATION OF EACH SEAT THAT RUNS IT: a fire is stamped with its schedule's conversation (`FirePartition`, which is `notify.ScheduleConversation` of its scope, scope id and name) as BOTH keys, so the fires that wait in a seat's inbox together run once and each fire's turn continues the session the schedule's last fire left on that seat's executor log; renaming a schedule starts it afresh and editing its task or its cron does not, and `org.ScheduleNameMaxBytes` holds every key under the log's bound (`TestTheLongestScheduleNameFitsTheLogsKey`) |

## The edges

| Package | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `api` | REST + the dashboard. Served INSIDE the engine's process and nowhere else: `crewlet run` builds it over the engine's own store, broker and coordination plane, and `New` refuses a missing one by name, because a narrower answer built around a nil (an omitted health field, a 503, an absent route) reads as deliberate and hides the wiring mistake. `NodeRuntime` is the seam it asks the engine through. EVERY REQUEST LEAVES THE GUARD CARRYING A PRINCIPAL — resolved, anonymous, or unknown — and the EXEMPTION LIST is the whole of what is not guarded (probes, webhooks on their own HMAC, the per-run token paths, the dashboard shell, the sign-in routes, and the sign-out of THIS session — which clears the cookie whatever the node can read, where guarded a node that could not read its identity estate answered it 503 before it ran, and which verifies every bearer it ends itself). There is no list of what IS: guarded is what a route is, so the always-guarded prefix list is gone and each surface states its authority as a VERB where it is enforced — which is why every surface `New` mounts, `/config`, `/secrets` and `/setup` included, is a `guardedMounter` whose routes go through `authz.Router`, and why the deployment's own controls (`/backup`, every `/worklet/retention*` route and the fleet broker's removals) are mounted there on `admin`. None of them decided anything before: the guard answers only whether somebody resolved, and a surface that relied on that opened itself to every signed-in reader the day sessions arrived. The query registry is where both transports meet that: one question, one declared POSTURE (`queries.Posture` — `Everybody()`, `Requires(admin|app)` or `DecidedBy(verb)`, whose answer decides record by record), and a REST route and a socket frame decided by the same check, so no question is reachable by choosing a channel — and a registration with a zero posture, a `Requires` of anything but admin or an app, or a `DecidedBy` of a verb the table does not know PANICS at wiring time, because a question nobody decided about is an ungated surface that ships looking deliberate — and so does a `DecidedBy` of a verb that asks a recent proof or a person present, since the socket has no code for either refusal, a walk in `internal/authz` holding the verbs an answer or a watch decides by inside itself to the same rule; a refusal travels as the decision whole (`queries.Refusal`, built only by `NewRefusal`) and both transports word it through `authz.RefusalFields`; a principal whose stage may not act is refused before any answer runs. THE OVERVIEW IS EVERYBODY'S (ADR-0033): the org chart, the agents' and executors' STATUS, spend, budgets, schedules, tools, health and `viewer` answer any resolved principal, while a call's or a run's BODY — prompts, responses, tool arguments, narration, `llm_history` payloads, an executor's task, question, reply and bridged calls — goes only to admin, to the seat's lead (`audit.seat.read`) and, for a run's question, to the person it is put to, through ONE mask per surface (`livestate.MaskCall`, `ExecutorEntry.For`, the executor key walk) that zeroes the body's versions and sets `body_withheld`, held by walks that fail on a field nobody classified; and a cross-app answer filters its rows through `authz.Shows`. Its refusal is three-valued for `iam.From`'s reason: an identity estate this node cannot read is `ErrUnavailable` with a Retry-After, a context no resolver touched is a plain FAULT (a route nobody wired through the guard never clears by waiting), and only a credential positively checked and refused is unauthorized. THE VIEWER IS THE CALLER: the principal travels in the context on both transports and no operator id rides beside it, and `viewer=` is gone from `work_items` and `work_views` — it had exactly one honest value, and any other was a free choice of whose pins, personal views and queue to read. CHAT'S QUESTIONS GO FURTHER (`queries/chat.go`): they take no handle at all — a room is read as the seat the principal acts as, the same `iam.ActorFor` a chat write's author comes from, so whoever may post in a room is exactly whoever is shown it — and each decides its own SEATED verb on the authority table before it reads anything, so a credential acting as itself is refused `unseated` rather than shown the company's rooms as nobody; the badges ride the rail from the coordination read state, and one that could not be read is `read_state: false` rather than a cursor at zero. A question that names somebody else's record resolves the name first — `iam.OwnerOf` through `Sources.Holders`, which `New` REQUIRES, so a login is its holder's record and never read literally, and only after the question's own verb has been decided on the unresolved login (`Sources.mayLook`), so a caller who leads nobody is refused before the directory is asked — and is decided by the authority table on what it resolved to, under the QUESTION'S OWN VERB — a person's queue by the owner-or-lead class through `Sources.Chart`, whose UNKNOWN answers 503 rather than a refusal, and a seat's trail (`agent_memory`, `agent_episode`, `memory_overview`, `executor_sessions`, `executor_session`) by `audit.seat.read`, its lead or admin — and a refusal carries the rule's `reason` and the `grants` that would have admitted the caller rather than a sentence written beside the rule — and which `New` REQUIRES, because the production wiring once left it out and every lead's read of a report's record was a 503 no retry could clear; it used to be "any operator credential", which made every Tier A token a reader of every seat's inbox. A token acts AS A SEAT only when the identity directory holds an ACTIVE MACHINE row under its login bound to one, and that seat is resolved against the running org through the SAME `session.ResolveSeat` a signed-in person's is (`auth.SeatBindings`) — `403 seat_unavailable` once the running company no longer holds it as a human seat, `503` on a node that runs no company yet — because the lookup it replaced returned the row's raw handle, so a token went on acting as a removed seat; an UNBOUND answer is served even by a stalled node, which is what keeps break-glass reachable — and a seat's contact block names no credential at all, because it says how to reach a person and not which credential they hold. A CHAT ROOM'S PRESENCE (who is viewing, typing, working) is the presence hub's (`internal/presence`, ADR-0038) like an artifact's: the chat room's `presence` frame (`room: "chat"`, `channel_id`) IS the join — a tab looks at one chat room at a time, so a frame naming another room moves the socket and an empty one leaves — admitted once `chatlet.Visible` lets its viewer see the room (the decision a committed frame takes, so a refusal leaves nothing and says nothing), pushed as `chat_presence` from the hub's fan-out to the sockets in the room and nobody else — its roster handed in the presence hub's delivery order (`presence.Hub.Join`'s hand, which places the socket and sends the roster under the chat hub's ONE LOCK, the lock every fan-out of the room's presence chooses its sockets and sends under), so a socket is shown a fan-out wholly before its roster or after it and nothing after the roster that took it out — and decided again by every committed record that narrows the room, which takes out whoever it shuts out with a roster naming nobody, and by every gap, which may have held such a record and so decides every socket in a room again — keeping one it cannot decide, where the record fails closed, because a gap is only the possibility of a change; a seat's working indicator is its agent member there (`SetStatus` touches, `ClearStatus` withdraws), raised on whichever node runs the turn and carried between nodes sealed. The unsigned fleet-wide scatter it replaced, `crewlet.chat.presence`, let anybody on the cluster port show anybody typing in any room. A batch the hub cannot keep up with is dropped and owes every screen a `chat_room_changed` naming no room, which is also how a gap in what the engine hears is told. The hub is the PROCESS's (`api.EngineChatLive`), attached to the engine after `New` on every node, and only an API mounted over it makes it say it serves sockets. AN UNSERVED SURFACE IS ONE TYPE (`Unserved`: its own code, its words, and when to ask THIS node again — zero where waiting clears nothing), read by `UnavailableOf` for both transports: a node with no company yet (`ErrNoCompany`, one value of it) was a sentinel with an arm of its own in each transport's mapping, and a node serving none of Gitlet now was answered over REST alone, by routes of its own — so a REST 503 and the socket's `unavailable` frame could say different things about when to come back. |
| `observe` | The observability edge, and the two routes are deliberately different: the STORE is written by a publish listener inline on the publishing node (no consumer group, so no two nodes can write one row); the PROJECTION is fed by an ephemeral per-caller broadcast. A node WITHOUT `data` writes no rows of its own — its store is deleted at every boot — so `Custody` publishes its events in batches onto a durable custody topic instead, buffered so a publish never waits and loud about what a full buffer drops, and every data node's `Keeper` takes them from ONE fleet-wide group. A group delivers a batch whose acknowledgement was lost again, to anybody, so a keeper writes a batch FIRST and claims it create-only in coordination SECOND: the winner keeps it, any other writer deletes its copy, and a crash between the two is settled from the node's `custody_unsettled` rows at its next pass — because a batch in two logs is a stateless node's spend the usage domain bills twice, and claimed first, a claimant that died before writing would hold a batch nobody wrote. A REDELIVERY OF A BATCH THIS NODE ALREADY SETTLED WRITES NOTHING (`custody_settled`, swept with the event log): written again it was in flight again, and its kept rows left every usage count until the claim answered a second time. And a keeper's stop LEAVES the group — stops taking batches, gives one in hand a second to settle, detaches — before the usage publisher's last flush, since every settle as kept makes rows count on this node's days |
| `eventfan` | The fleet's TURN-LEVEL HISTORY, read from every data node at query time (ADR-0021). An event is written once, inline, to the store of the data node that published it or keeps it in custody for a node without `data`, so no one store is the company's history: `events`, `event`, `event_series`, `trace`, `turn`, `turns`, `phases`, `notification_outcomes`, an MCP server's recent calls (`tool_calls`, read out of the phase records' tool logs, found by their `mcp_servers` tag), a seat's history and the live projection's boot seed (its feed, its spend window through `phase_tokens`, each seat's last turn) are asked of every live data node over the queue's EPHEMERAL verbs on `crewlet.observe.read` — the asker reads its own store directly and in parallel, and the scatter lasts until every node the roster NAMES has answered, never a count of replies, because every node serves, one the roster does not hold among them (a draining node gives its presence back first and serves until it stops) — and merged, with ONE `coverage{nodes:[{id,answered,error}],complete}` on every answer naming a node that did not answer inside the two-second `FleetReadBudget` (which the `history_partial` alarm borrows). The merges are PURE and each is exact for disjoint stores for a reason it states: a keyset page stops at the newest point any FULL part stopped at (a reply cut to fit the transport is full and short), a histogram's window is pinned to the asker's clock before bars are summed, and `turns` is TWO scatters — every data node's page, then every data node's share of exactly the turns listed — because the node a turn is selected on is not always the only node holding it. The interface `internal/api/queries` reads it through returns a coverage from every method, so a bare `*store.EventLog` does not compile there. A seat's history is asked by its AGENT ID and never by a role name, and every question the reply is drawn against carries the ONE instant it is answered at (`q.At`), so a node never labels its part by its own clock. A departed node's detail is gone, by design; the aggregates survive it in `usage`. `eventfantest` certifies it on the twin and on a three-member cluster |
| `tokens` | Rolls LLM spend into the breakdown a dashboard renders — by phase, model, provider entry, worker and seat, plus a per-turn tail on the LIVE window only — and its time axis. ONE IMPLEMENTATION is the whole point: this aggregation had three copies once, and a refresh routinely disagreed with the page it replaced. TWO INPUTS, one shape: the live projection's spend records (`Aggregate`) and every NAMED window's company days from the replicated `usage` domain (`FoldDaily`, `BucketDaily`), which is why a named window has no turn and no hour — a day's row holds neither, and inventing them from this node's event log is the one-node answer ADR-0020 replaced. A phase chart draws FOUR bands folded once in `PhaseBand` — a launch of an executor's run is no fifth: both producers file its record under the executor's own phase (`PhaseExecute`) — a window is at most `MaxSpendRangeDays` (90) and one reaching past the 181-day horizon is REFUSED rather than drawn short. `calls` is PROVIDER CALLS on every bucket (`PhaseCalls` is the one rule both producers count a phase by: a phase's rounds, and NONE for the executor's own record — every executor is its harness's run, so the engine made no call for it, and counting the record's one round put two calls on every turn that nobody made; `LaunchCalls` is a launch's: its harness's own turns as reported on its `executor_collected` record), and a TURN'S COST is defined here once (`Record.InTurn`): its phases, its executor's launches and its in-turn auxiliary spend, never the reflection after it. A leaf in everything but the calendar (`period`), because both the live projection and the query surface need it. A seat's band is keyed on its AGENT ID and a unit's on its KEY, each carrying a `label` drawn from the company as the caller holds it now, because a name is prose two seats may share — keyed on it, two namesakes pooled their spend into one row — and a PERSON's auxiliary spend is a row of its own, keyed on the HUMAN SEAT'S HANDLE, since it was charged to no agent |
| `coalesce` | HOW A NODE PUBLISHES A RECORD IT MAKES MANY TIMES A SECOND, once for every such record (ADR-0008): each occurrence FOLDED into one bucket per key under one lock, every bucket SEALED into one event a flush — its id and instant fixed, so a retry is the same event the store's (time, id) key collapses — and published OFF THE CALLER'S PATH, since no publish ever runs under the lock: a broker electing a leader or short of its quorum holds up no request, where a publish inline waits for a replicated, fsynced acknowledgement, up to the client's five-second default. Flushed every `FlushInterval` (15 s, the usage domain's cadence, held equal by its suite, since every record a ledger carries is counted by a usage day), on an owner's own moment (`FlushWhere`) and at the stop. The first refusal ends a flush, and what it held back is kept, MERGED BY SEAL ORDER — never put in front, which once made the bound drop a turn's fresh records as the oldest — up to `MaxPending` (4 096, under three megabytes), past which the oldest is dropped and said with what it held. Two owners, `auxspend` (auxiliary spend) and `code/readaudit` (who read a unit's repository), each saying only what its records are (`Records`: the key, the seal, what a lost one costs) |
| `auxspend` | What the seats' AUXILIARY model spends, recorded — the `Use` every caller of the auxiliary seam states (stage, purpose, turn; the zero value REFUSED), the per-turn `Tally` a turn's work item is charged from (ADR-0022), the turn's own `Budget` meter a turn-stage call is charged THROUGH and asks before it is made — because a post-charge beside the meter left the window it filled unseen, and the turn's next round was sent, billed and refused — and the node's `Ledger`, which coalesces each call into one `auxiliary_spend` record per (stage, seat or person, turn, purpose, model, provider entry, company day) per flush. RECORDED INDEPENDENTLY OF THE COUNTER at the one seam that charges it, because the counter exists only where a coordination store and a budget scope do, and a figure a person reads must depend on neither. The ledger is a `coalesce` ledger, so its fold, flush, sealed backlog and stop are that package's: flushed every 15 s, for a turn before its end is published and before its reflection pass's sentinel, and at the stop — ordered after every producer of auxiliary calls and before the custody flush and the stream close — and a refused record kept sealed up to `coalesce.MaxPending`, so a process that dies during a broker outage loses that backlog as well as its open buckets |
| `tracing` | The OpenTelemetry wiring: ONE TracerProvider, built from the standard `OTEL_*` environment (never a Tier A block), and the conversion between OTel's `context.Context` carrier and the `trace_id`/`span_id`/`parent_span_id` the event envelope has always had. The provider is installed UNCONDITIONALLY and only the exporter is optional, so ids reach the event store whether or not a collector exists — and its own `init` installs a working one, because OTel's built-in default is a no-op that passes the parent's span context through and would silently reinstate the bug this package removed |
| `notify` | The backend-neutral notification spine — conversation keys, digest coalescing, party resolution, the rate valve, and BOTH DIRECTIONS across a chat surface: the working indicator writes, and `ThreadReader`/`ThreadReaders` read a thread back for the turn-start block. Each direction is a per-backend seam with a fan-out that routes on the trigger's own `transport`, because a company runs two chat surfaces and a caller holding one backend's reader silently reads none. An indicator is posted as a `StatusPost` (handle, channel, thread, the text, and the NEWEST turn holding it, which a backend that can name a turn links to), and Chatlet shows it as the seat's agent member of the room's presence rather than a message. `ThreadOf` is deliberately NOT `ConversationOf`: one answers where a reply lands (a top-level message anchors on its own id), the other what was already said (a message with no thread has no answer). A SCHEDULE IS A CONVERSATION nobody replies into: its key is spelled once (`ScheduleConversation`, under `SchedulePrefix`, a slash no source's colon-namespaced key starts with) and recognised once (`Scheduled`), which tells a fire's run in the schedule's words, and `Derived` refuses it as it refuses the per-event fallback, so the dispatcher never offers a fire to a parked run as a reply and the runs board never says one is answerable in chat; internal/sandbox, which notify reaches through internal/tracing, is told the answer by its caller. Built before any vendor sat on it, because a spine built after its first vendor has that vendor welded into it. AN ENGINE-HOSTED SOURCE'S SENDER ID IS THE SEAT'S HANDLE (the tracker's, the knowledge base's, chat's, Gitlet's), and the registry is built with those sources DECLARED as namespaces whose ids are handles (`NewRegistry`'s `handleNamespaces`, the engine's one `firstPartySources` list, held to its native parsers by a test), so `ByExternalID` on one answers `ByHandle` and nothing can be registered there: read through a registry that did not know, every person on a native surface was an outside party — the learning profile filed them under a platform id, the thread block fenced a colleague as `external`, and a turn a person's comment woke was a stranger's, refused every artifact read the requester ceiling would have allowed them. EVERY WAKE'S BODY IS FENCED BY THE SPINE, never by a prompt (ADR-0040): `Render`, the one caller of `Prompt.Build`, hands a prompt the body already inside a fence, so a prompt that renders it in six openers cannot render it bare in any. What the body is and who wrote it is the ninth question a source answers (`Prompt.Provenance`), and most answer from what their parser STATED (`Stated`, over `BodySourceField`, `BodyAuthorField` and a first-party record's `BodyAuthorKindField`): an author only where the payload says one person wrote every word — a comment or a review just written, a message, an item's text on the event that created it — and otherwise nobody, which reads `external` on a vendor's surface, because the person who caused an event (who assigned the issue) is not who wrote its body; Worklet, Doclet and Chatlet read it as a colleague's (`StatedHosted`, `ChatPrompt.Hosted`, `Transcript.Hosted`: `Provenance.Hosted`), the one rule for a surface the engine hosts (`provenance.TrustForHosted`), as the same text reads through a search hit or a read tool (`engine.TestEveryWakeSurfaceReadsAnUnnamedWriterByWhoHostsIt`), and a first-party record naming its writer by kind alone (the engine, an operator credential) names that kind. A first-party writer the chart no longer holds is the kind its record stated (`FirstPartyAuthor`). The delivery mints a token for that wake alone (`Inbound.Fence`, recorded as `types.ExternalNotification.FenceBoundary`), because no turn exists yet to lend one, a coalesced burst's digest moves every earlier body's fence onto the latest's token, and the turn moves them onto its own (`provenance.Rekey`, in `engine.DescribeTrigger`), escaping everything else a trigger carries as a tool answer's other strings are; `engine.TestEveryWakeSurfaceFencesWhatSomebodyWrote` holds every surface the engine hosts or integrates to it, and `engine.TestEveryPromptBuilderIsAWakeSurface` walks the tree for every type that builds a trigger (a `Build(notify.Inbound, …)` method) and holds each to one of those surfaces. `SalientLabels` is that same answer for a DELIVERED notification's salient body, one `provenance.Label` per message in the order the turn reads them, and `SalientLabel` their merge (`provenance.Merge`), which the turn-start judgements read the turn's ask under: a merged burst names every constituent's writers at the least trust any earns (`engine.TestTheTurnsAskIsFencedAsItsTriggerIs`). `Prompt.WakesActor` is asked with the whole notification, since Worklet answers it from the routing reason on each recipient's copy rather than the event type every copy shares. A human seat's contact identities are registered only while the person the IDENTITY DIRECTORY binds to it may be reached: a `Standing` is ONE reading of the directory, applied whole to the registry being built, and its zero value is CHART-ONLY, which no running node builds from: a node that HOLDS THE ESTATE reads its OWN identity rows, from boot, company or none, and a node WITHOUT `data` reads the same reading through the estate router (`SeatHolders`, floored on the identity log, so a data node behind answers unknown rather than an old binding) — because routing by the chart attributes a suspended person's word to their seat for every delivery a node wins, and a node that has NEVER read a standing withholds every human seat until it does. The zero value is what an engine with no directory at all builds from, which is `crewlet validate` and a test. A binding names its seat by its handle (ADR-0013), so a reading finds the seat exactly as the request path finds the same binding's seat. What AGENTS are shown follows the same reading: a turn pins the live registry's withholding beside its org (`turnctx.Turn.Withheld`), so a lead's roster and `lookup_colleague` leave out exactly the people an inbound message would not be attributed to, and neither says why. `active`, `invited` and `enrolling` route; `suspended`, `retired`, a removal and a stage this build cannot name withhold, and an unreadable directory is an error rather than a reading, so a caller never hands every suspended person's seat back to the chart over an outage. The CHAT PROMPT reads the same addressed rule the indicator and the delivery check do (`addressOf`), and on an addressed message states that verdict IN PLACE OF the triage: the triage tells an unaddressed seat that silence beats noise, which on an addressed message is the one answer the decoder refuses. A FIRST-PARTY notice STATES who wrote its change (`Inbound.Writer` onto the wake and each coalesced constituent, `FirstPartyWriter`): the tracker and the knowledge base have no namespace an id resolves in, and the KIND their record holds says whether the actor is a seat's handle, a credential's login or a node's name — never the spelling, which is the same for all three. A CREDENTIAL'S writer carries its login and the apps the node that took its write recorded beside it (`NotificationWriter.Login`/`Apps`, from Worklet's and Doclet's `MutationRecord.ActorApps`), and `FirstPartyWriter` takes the apps as a parameter, so no producer names a credential's write without what a turn it wakes may use for it (ADR-0109) THE PARTITION FUNCTION SPLITS THE STAMPED KEY BY WRITER (`KeyOf`, `WriterSeparator`): one turn works for one writer (ADR-0109), so two people in one thread, or a person and a stranger, are two partitions, each held to its own writer, the writer read from what every producer already sends (a first-party notice's writer, the actor, else the sender), while `KeyOfAll` stays the stamped, thread-grained key a merged event and a parked run's batch carry. |
| `backup` | A restorable copy of everything a node holds, taken from INSIDE the engine because that is the only place both estates are reachable: the store file is locked to this process and the driver refuses a second opener, and the embedded broker binds no socket for any outside tool to dial. The store copy is `VACUUM INTO` (the backup API is stubbed and plain `VACUUM` is behind an experimental flag) taken by `store.DB.Backup` as ONE MOMENT holding every commit that returned before it began — which the trim hold leans on, since it pins the log at the position the node stood at just before the copies, and a copy older than that would leave the records between them pinned by nothing — and is VERIFIED before it counts. A copy holds its file's write-ahead log for its whole run, so before it pins or copies anything a backup checks each database's own volume has room for the log its copy will hold back there (`store.DB.CopyHoldsBack`, the last copy's measure), and refuses otherwise: the node commits to that volume and would stop once the log filled it; the copies themselves land in the operator's directory and are not counted there, since nothing tells two volumes of one pool apart and counting them on every live volume would refuse every backup to a disk of its own. The streams — mailboxes and every coordination bucket alike, since a bucket IS a stream — go over the JetStream wire API, because the vendored client has no snapshot call at all. A stream is copied WITH its consumers, and the broker abandons a snapshot when one of them ends mid-copy, which every coordination listing does (an ephemeral watch consumer); so a stream is snapshotted again when the consumer the broker names is one it no longer holds, five attempts in all (`backup_stream_retaken`), and every other abandonment fails the backup. The MANIFEST IS THE CLAIM: written last, and a directory without one is the debris of a run that did not finish rather than a partial backup. The objects the copy's Required rows name are WALKED (a Retired or Derived row's object is never copied, counted or asked after — on `nats` its bytes ride the bucket's snapshot uncounted, ADR-0081 — and each walk is built for `objstore.PassBackup`, so one handed such a table refuses it), never gathered — `objstore.MergeWalks` over the copy, a page of each table held, a key two rows name de-duplicated against the one before — and carried thirty-two at a time on `s3` (`backupFetchConcurrency`: a first copy is bound by each GET's first byte rather than the link, so the depth is Little's law over S3's 100–200 ms, measured at its lower end — `BenchmarkCarry` measured the large model's first copy at about five hours sixteen wide and three thirty-two wide, a 1 Gbit/s link's worth, and at the upper end it is about four (arithmetic) — under a twentieth of the prefix's GET rate and at the bucket's own transport's warm connections — s3obj's clone of httpx's, HTTP/1.1, `httpx.MaxIdleConnsPerHost` of them) or asked after thirty-two at a time on `nats` (`streamCheckConcurrency`, the audit's depth), each a closed loop that the first object the store still does not answer for after `fetchAttempts` (four, within one read's budget, in the same slot) ends. THE OBJECTS FOLLOW THE LOG (ADR-0082): a restore brings the copy back at P and replays each declaring log to the last sequence L its snapshot captured — the snapshot is point-in-time at the state its answer states — so the backup also reads (P, L] of each log, and the records the copy's applier deferred, through each declaration's `Records`, and carries every object they name; it never waits for an applier or reads the live rows, whose read would land past L. A record it cannot read that may write a declared table refuses it (`objstore.ErrRecordUnreadable`, `409 record_unreadable`), judged from what every build reads of the record, never from what this build's applier does with its kind; every record is read through the verified log, so one signed under a key this node does not hold refuses it too (`statelog.ErrRecordUnverified`, `409 record_unverified`) and one no key of the fleet opens is a `500`; a log trimmed past the copy or a hole between P and L (`ErrLogGap`, `503 log_gap`), or a copy keyed to an earlier instance of the log (`409 log_recreated`), refuses it too, each answered with a hint saying what to do; the object stream is snapshotted after every log; and an object it could not carry is LOST only where the restored rows name it. ONE AT A TIME PER NODE (`ErrBackupRunning`, `409 backup_running`): the trim hold is keyed on the node, so two at once would share one pin and the first to finish would release the other's. `backuptest` restores a backup's stream snapshots into a bare broker — the runbook's `nats stream restore`, for the suite that proves a restored node serves what it backed up — handing each stream back the configuration its snapshot recorded, verbatim, because the stamp in it is the stream's identity (`statelog.CreatedAtKey`) |
| `maintenance` | The retention sweep for the tables that answer "recently" rather than "ever" — fire claims, channel membership, counterparty profiles, each state-log domain's OPERATION LEDGER, the coordination store's REMOVAL MARKERS (a bucket no clock ages keeps every delete marker, and every listing that meets one re-reads it from the leader), and a removed human seat's CHAT READ STATE (its bucket has no age either, so a record whose seat the company the fleet is pointed at has lacked for a day — stamped when a sweep first observes the absence, the mailbox retirement's grace so a seat restored inside it gets back its mail and its rooms together — is forgotten by a compare-and-set that checks the stamp; the roster is the HUMAN seats, because the record is the seat's and a person leaving a seat the company still has leaves it to the next holder; a roster that cannot be read forgets nobody). Every one of their migrations says they are swept and ships the index a range delete needs — a table with a documented retention and no sweep grows for the life of the deployment, which is what the `<domain>_ops` tables did until `StatelogJobs` existed. A ledger horizon is the DOMAIN's, and a domain may declare a SHORTER one per subject KIND whose writers never re-ask late (`OpsHorizon.Kinds`, a job of its own) — the identity estate's sessions go in an hour where everything else keeps the month, a range over the stored subject on an index only that domain ships. Every horizon is a FUNCTION read at each sweep (`Horizon`, `Fixed` for a constant), so a retention a revision changes is the next sweep's rather than the next boot's. A fleet singleton, because N nodes scanning the same rows is waste rather than corruption — except where the rows are a table each node owns its own copy of, which is what a job's `Scope` of `NodeLocal` is for: swept under the singleton, such a table is tidied on one node and grows for ever on every other, and that looks exactly like a sweep that works to whoever checks the node it ran on |
| `mattermost`, `slack`, `gitlab`, `github`, `jira`, `confluence`, `datadog`, `cloudflare`, `expo`, `digitalocean`, `scaleway`, `googlecloud`, `atlassian`, `aws`, `ssh` | The vendors. Each contributes only what is genuinely its own: a client, a parser, a transport, a prompt, a provisioning reconcile, and no more, which is why Jira has no transport (an agent writes through its own MCP tools) and why its reconcile and GitHub's report rather than mint (neither vendor issues a credential on a provisioner's behalf). Datadog is the ALERT one and the shape shows it: a monitor is addressed to nobody, so it routes on the monitor's own TAGS with a company-wide fallback seat, and its deliveries cannot be signed at all. Scaleway is the one whose provisioner reaches its whole Organization: no condition can keep a key that manages applications to the agents' applications, so what bounds an agent is its fixed level table and the ledger's application IDs, and the connect form says so. Google Cloud is the one with no provisioner credential to paste: the engine mints its own ES256 key, the owner uploads only its public half to a workload identity provider, and the provisioner it impersonates is contained by three conditions on each project, one hasOnly list per level, so every write touches one list; projects are discovered from those grants rather than listed, an agent's token is issued at use and never sealed, and every read after the engine's own write waits through one bound within which a stale answer is never drift. SSH is the one with no vendor at all: the engine is the certificate authority, servers trust only its public line, and a seat's level and hosts are the document alone, so its access sync takes no step (ADR-0105). Slack is the one with no reconciler (its apps are created from the command line), so it is registered teardown-only and carries no reconcile status. A vendor's PROMPT states only what the engine knows and the model cannot: why the seat is reading this, the item by the reference a person would paste, the vendor facts (mention markup, subscription mechanics, what a merge or a close means) and how a seat declines what it HOLDS on that surface (reassign the item assigned to it, hand a review request on), never offered to a seat asked about somebody else's item, which is not its to move, while "stay silent" is shown only to a seat the prompt's own `Addressed` reads as NOT asked. How to review a diff or work an alert is the model's own, and that an ask may not end in silence is the executor's contract and the decoder's refusal, so neither is restated per vendor |
| `origin` | WHERE A FAILURE LEFT THE ENGINE'S OWN CODE: `defer origin.Stamp(&err)` wraps the first non-nil error with the deferring function's name, read off the runtime's frame and never the error, and only for a function under the module's `internal/` tree; its file is a base name. THE DEEPEST STAMP WINS, so a mid-level stamp is a fallback for failures nobody below stamped. TRANSPARENT: the message is the error's own and `errors.Is`/`errors.As` see through it, which is why a stamp goes only where every caller uses them, never `==` or a direct type assertion. A failed turn's record carries the stamp (`error_function`, `error_file`). The rejected alternatives (an error's type, a message's prefix, a program counter in every constructor) are in the package doc. |
| `issuereport` | Opt-in ANONYMOUS REPORTS of the engine's own defects, filed by a relay as GitHub issues (ADR-0101). THE ALLOWLIST IS A TYPE: `Report` holds no plain string, each is a named type a validating constructor makes, because a redactor over an error message fails open on the words a company writes, and `TestAReportHoldsNoPlainString` fails on a field added later. One `Catalogue` table, exported to `schema/issue-report-catalogue.json` for the relay to vendor. A class's shape is immutable after a reporting tag (`schema/issue-report-history/`), and a site is a stable token a test maps to a live function, so an older release's reports keep validating. Detection is a publish listener over the typed failure records, the dispatcher's dead-letter hook and every panic `panics` contains, its counters this node's memory, each subject hashed on arrival. A panic in a package that parses input before it is authenticated (`BeforeAuthentication`), or one served on an unguarded route, is reported with its site alone, never its frames. A CRASH IS THE NEXT PROCESS'S TO REPORT (`NextStart`): a copy of the applied setting beside the node's database arms the runtime's crash output, and the first revision the next start applies reads it (on) or deletes it unread (off), as it does a release's failed migration (`store.MigrationError`, closed values only); a crash with a frame in code an outsider or a model's arguments reach is held in the record (`held`), never sent. The SENT RECORD is `coord.IssueReports`, one compare-and-set record per fingerprint, because every node detects and one may send. It is off until a revision turns it on, and a revision that turns it off cancels a send under way. ONLY A BUILD ANYBODY CAN READ SENDS (`Origin`: a tag, a `main-` stamp, a module pseudo-version or a `go install`), because a development build's defect is often its developer's own unmerged change: any other binary stays inert with the setting on. AN OUTAGE IS NOT A DEFECT: the turn loop's `error` kind is what nothing classified, an environment condition being its own kind (`builtin.ConditionKind`), and a signal an outage can cause (`Signal.Shadowed`) counts nothing while an alarm in `ShadowAlarms` stands anywhere in the fleet, read every alarm beat off this node's tracker and every node's presence beat (a node without `data` evaluates none) and failing closed when it cannot be read; a hand-back (`Signal.HandBack`) counts nothing while a node drains or the live nodes run more than one build (`coord.NodeStatus.Build`). A panic is never shadowed. |

| `httpx` | The ONE outbound HTTP transport. Leaving `http.Client.Transport` nil is not "the defaults": it is `http.DefaultTransport`, whose `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` is **2, process-wide**, which seven vendor clients were silently sharing. One transport rather than one per client: a per-client clone is strictly worse than the default, since each keeps a private pool and reuses nothing between them. EVERY outbound client is built here, the operator CLI's included; a bare `&http.Client{}` outside this package is the bug, and a round tripper that wraps another takes `httpx.Transport()` as its base, which is the shape that slips through because it names no client at all. `Customized` is for a client whose TLS or protocol genuinely differs — the bucket's, over HTTP/1.1 alone. A proxy the operator set is dialled as itself and only an address written into the URL is judged before it, since the proxy resolves a name on its own. An address the OPERATOR configured stays on `httpx.Client`, because a private one there is the deployment they chose. The rule has three doors: `NewRule(resolver)`, the `Rule` on the network of the resolver a host is resolved with (the zero `Rule`, and a nil one, refuse every address), whose `Public(ctx, addr)` the guard asks of each address it connects to; `ResolvePublic(ctx, resolver, host)`, for a dialer that hands an address to another program to connect to (Gitlet's git), which returns a host's addresses only when every one is public; and `Public(ip)`, for a caller holding an address and making no dial (the configuration's validation, `github.Deliverable`), the verdict on a network that names no NAT64 prefix. An IPv4 address is public unless it is in a block IANA's special-purpose registry reserves (private, loopback, link-local with the cloud metadata address, carrier-grade NAT, documentation, benchmarking, the deprecated 6to4 relay anycast) or multicast, and one written in IPv6 form is judged as itself. An IPv6 address that carries a zone (`fe80::1%eth0`) is refused before any block is asked: no host on the internet is named with one, and netip's own predicates judge a zoned address as if it had none, so a rule judging its bits alone would step around every block. An IPv6 address in a NAT64 prefix is judged by the IPv4 address it carries and by nothing else: the well-known `64:ff9b::/96` always, and the network-specific prefixes RFC 7050 discovery reads from the same resolver's answer for `ipv4only.arpa`. That lookup is made at most once a dial or a resolve, never kept, and ONLY for an address whose verdict its answer can change: an IPv6 one in global unicast or in `64:ff9b:1::/48`, where a named prefix counts (below). No record means none; any other failure refuses each address that needed the answer, with the resolver's error, so the rule is never applied on a guess. An IPv4 address, one in the well-known prefix and one the allowlist refuses elsewhere are judged without it, so an IPv4-only host costs no lookup beyond its own and is never refused for a lookup it did not need; `ResolvePublic` refuses a host one of whose addresses is not public with `ErrNotPublic` even when another could not be judged, whatever order the resolver answers in. A prefix the resolver names counts only where its word cannot widen the rule into a network that is not on the internet: inside the allowlist below, where judging an address by what it carries can only refuse more, or inside `64:ff9b:1::/48`, the block RFC 8215 reserves for a network's own translation prefix. Named anywhere else (unique-local, link-local, documentation, `::/96`) it is ignored and its addresses stay refused, so a DNS64 network translates through `64:ff9b::/96`, a prefix in `64:ff9b:1::/48` or one in its own global unicast space, or its dialer reaches the host through a proxy its caller trusts: through a translator on a unique-local prefix the rule reaches no host that has only an IPv4 address. Any other IPv6 address is public ONLY in global unicast (`2000::/3`) outside `2001::/23`, the two documentation blocks and 6to4: an ALLOWLIST, because a list of reserved IPv6 blocks cannot be completed (IANA keeps reserving more) and missed every form that carries an IPv4 address (NAT64, 6to4, Teredo, IPv4-compatible). Every caller that refuses an address asks it rather than keeping a list of its own, which would drift from the others unnoticed |

It walks every Go file through `sourcetree` and counts each reference to those eight in TEST CODE — every `_test.go` file and every file of a package whose directory name ends in `test`, computed rather than listed — through the file's own name for `time`, an alias, a dot import or a function value included, and every `Sub` whose receiver's TYPE is `time.Time` — never told by a name, since any expression can be one — typed through `sourcetree`'s `TypeCheck` for the packages whose test code spells `Sub` and only those (a `Sub` in a file this platform does not build cannot be typed, and is refused). A reference leaves the class only three ways, each stated rather than inferred, because a duration, a shape or a name cannot tell a liveness bound from a claim: inside a synctest bubble (`synctest.Test`'s or `Run`'s literal, or one handed to a BUBBLE RUNNER, a function that hands its parameter whole to synctest), inside a `//fixedwait:bubble` helper, which is VERIFIED AT EVERY USE (a helper is a function its callers choose where to run), or under a `//fixedwait:liveness`, `//fixedwait:simulated <reason>` or `//fixedwait:bench` marker on a wait, or a `//fixedwait:measure <reason>` on an elapsed reading that decides nothing (logged, reported, a poll's own deadline), or a `//fixedwait:stated <reason>` on a `time.Time`'s `Sub` between instants no wall clock separates (the test's own, or a clock it controls; never `Since` or `Until`, which read now), each covering only its own shape — a line holding a wait and a reading takes one marker above and one trailing — and ONE line its place decides (trailing code, that line; alone, the line under it). A bubble runner is matched within its own package clause and never through a local of its name, and a method with an exported name cannot be declared bubble-only, since it is reached through interfaces and embeddings where no name says so. Everything else is held to `allowed.go`, an inventory keyed by file and function (so an unrelated edit never churns it), counted BY SHAPE (its fixed waits and its readings of elapsed time each held to their own fields, so neither stands in for the other) by the survey's categories (an elapsed bound among them) and naming the piece of crewlet/crewlet#734 that removes it: it ONLY SHRINKS, because an entry recording more than its function holds fails as surely as a reference no entry covers, and adding one is the decision, as in `skipgate`. A malformed or stale marker, a bench marker outside a function taking a `*testing.B`, a marker over only references it does not cover, and a bubble declaration off a function's doc or over no wait are refused; a wait that only steps the clock past a stamped instant is counted as a clock step, whose fix is a clock the test controls. The package doc holds the house patterns (#634, #644 and #652 a bubble; #642 a witness signal, a fence or the producer's own count; #646 a wait on the parked state) and the gaps it does not see: `context.WithTimeout` windows, a `Sub` reached through an interface or a type parameter, a fake outside a `…test` directory (s3fake, until piece 9 renames it) and a literal written in a bubble that runs after it. |
| `clocktest` | INSTANTS WHOSE TWO CLOCK READINGS HAVE PARTED, for tests of code that measures time across them: `AfterSleep` (the wall reading moved, the monotonic one not, as a host that slept reads its clock) and `Parted` (each moved by its own amount, as a wall clock stepped back does too). Go compares two instants that both carry a monotonic reading on that reading alone, so code that holds such an instant against something counting on the wall clock (a vendor's reset, a lease the store expires) answers wrongly after a sleep, and only a forged instant can show it: no exported call moves one reading without the other, so the wall seconds are written in place and the forgery checks that it moved exactly what it meant to, failing with the layout it assumes named. A leaf over the standard library, imported only by tests |
| `solo` | WHICH TEST PACKAGES NEED THE RUNNER TO THEMSELVES, as a declaration rather than a list. A package imports it from `TestMain` and `internal/solo/partition` derives both halves of the suite from that, so `make test` / `make test-solo` / ci.yml share ONE computed answer instead of three hand-maintained copies of a `grep -v`. Its roster guard is what makes the declaration self-maintaining, and it fails in BOTH directions: a package standing up a multi-member broker without declaring (the flake) and a package declaring without needing to (the flake-suppressant). The predicate is exact rather than approximate: the cluster harness's ENTIRE exported surface is four multi-member constructors, so importing it IS forming a quorum. The package doc is also where every alternative's measurement lives (a build tag hides files from `go vet` and golangci-lint and can drop a package from `go list` entirely, `-short` skips nothing on its own, a custom flag kills every test binary that does not define it, `-skip` leaves `[no tests to run]` and exit 0), and every one of them fails SILENTLY, which is why this is an import and not a tag. `partition` also ORDERS the parallel half from measured seconds (`-weights`): longest first, because `go test` starts package runs strictly in command-line order and alphabetical order started the three longest packages last; the solo half runs at `-p 1`, where no order ends it sooner. It DEALS a half across CI's runners (`-shard I/N`, longest-processing-time, every package in exactly one shard, asserted on every call) and MERGES the shards' timings into the next run's weights (`merge`, refusing a package two shards timed). Weights decide order and which shard, NEVER membership of a half; an unmeasured package weighs its half's median |
| `e2e` | The gates only a whole running node can answer: a real engine on a real embedded stream, the real API in front of it, a real turn driven by a scripted model, and the dashboard's OWN modules consuming the frames that come out. Nothing is stubbed but the vendor endpoint, because what it exists to catch is a misunderstanding BETWEEN two components that each implement consistently with their own tests — an event shape the projection does not key on, a slice the client does not read — which no suite of one component can see. It has no exported surface, and it forms clusters, so it runs in `make test-solo`. | `docsgate` | The tree's prose held to the files it points at: every relative markdown link names a file that exists, every `#anchor` names a heading its target renders under GitHub's slug, and every page under `docs/` is in `docs/index.md` — the docs site's navigation. It reads this tree through `sourcetree.Walk`, so a nested checkout's stale copy of a page is never judged as this one. TEST-ONLY, and scoped to markdown on purpose: a dashboard address (`#/worklet/ENG-42`) is a ROUTE, which only the dashboard's resolver can evaluate, so `dashboard/src/app/links.test.ts` holds those (and every pointer at a `dashboard-design.md` heading, which lives mostly in code) rather than a second copy of the route table here. A link is never followed across the network: whether somebody else's page exists is not a property of this tree |
| `docslinks` | Test-only, like `docsgate`, and it certifies the links INTO the documentation site rather than between files: every address on the docs site that this repository carries — in the docs and the skill it publishes, the dashboard a person clicks through, the schemas an editor resolves, the code and the process files — names a page the site builds under its product and version segment, because the site forwards no path it used to serve and a link outside that shape is a 404 however it once resolved. It lives under `internal/` because the site copies `schema/` and `skills/` verbatim and serves them, so beside the skill it guarded it was itself published |

Several lists exist twice by necessity — the dashboard is a separate build in a separate language and cannot import a Go identifier — and each copy has drifted at least once, silently: a chip for a category no event carries filters a log down to nothing and reads as a quiet engine. The check belongs on the engine side because the engine owns the value. KEYED ON THE DECLARATION, NEVER A PATH, so a screen moving is invisible and the only two failures it reports are the ones that matter — nothing declares it, or two declarations do, in one file or in two. KEYED ON THE SYNTAX, NEVER THE LAYOUT: the source is SCANNED — strings, comments, template literals, regular expressions and JSX prose each recognised for what they are — and `Literal`, `Scalar`, `Union`, `Interface`, `Calls` and `Property` (one row of a table keyed by name) read tokens, because every regular expression they replaced was a claim about how prettier lays a declaration out, and one that stops matching does not fail, it matches LESS. What is not a literal (a spread, a computed key, a union member that is not a string, an expression where one value was expected) is refused by name rather than skipped. ONE REGISTRY, BOTH WAYS: `Contract()` names every declaration a gate reads, its reader and its ONE owning gate; a reader refuses a name the table does not carry, and `contract_test.go` refuses a row that does not resolve to exactly one declaration or whose gate does not read it.
